If you recognize your own source, then the ocean of birth and death is itself the gate of nirvana; there is not even a hair’s breadth of difference."
The Dharma acts as an obstruction and a hindrance, because this is a single dharma and not two dharmas. What is the root-source of oneself? Zhaozhou said:
"Before the world existed, this nature already existed; when the world perishes, this nature does not perish.
At that time, a monk asked: "What is this nature? Zhaozhou said: "The four great elements and the five aggregates. The monk said: "This is..."
"Ruined! What is this nature? Zhaozhou said, "The four great elements and the five aggregates. This monk was so intent on gazing at the moon in the sky that he lost the pearl in his hand.
Zhaozhou’s heart bears no grudge against others, and his face shows no shame.

Do you know where Zhaozhou does not bear a grudge? Listen further to this verse: "The four great elements and the five aggregates, Coming and going, going and coming, Like clouds suddenly appearing in the void."
Like thunder during a drought, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it is silent and profound, never departing from its very place.
Holding up his whisk, he said: "Do you understand? You must not fail the mountain monk."

The disciple Huang Taiyong offered the memorial of his deceased parents and requested a small discourse before the spirit. The Master said: "In the three realms, rising and sinking have no separate dharma;
it is merely because the power of karma arranges them. Karma arises from the mind and originally has no self-nature; it is like the empty flowers seen by diseased eyes that appear to differ.
If one can awaken to and enter the principle of no-self-nature, one may swallow the waters of the West River in a single gulp—this is the original face."
It is self-evident. Where else could one seek birth and death? As for this principle of no-nature—how is it realized?
Black as the sun, bright as lacquer; the great earth has waves and billows, yet the four seas have not a single drop. *Tu!* For now, turn toward this very place.
"Directly transcend and depart.

[This was] a small discourse (*xiaocan*). The Master said: "Today, the disciple Zhu Taiyun of Wenzhou has specifically ascended Mount Gu at the Buddha’s Birthday to invite the assembly of monks to recite the Buddha’s name, in order to dedicate the merit for the rebirth of his deceased parents and kinsmen in the Pure Land. He further requests the mountain..."
Monks, when preaching the Dharma to guide others, you must know that the entirety of the ten directions is this Land of Ultimate Bliss;
where, then, is there a world of the five turbidities? The entirety of the ten directions is one's own self;
where, then, is there Amitābha Buddha? If you can truly see through to this point, then your father, mother, ancestors, and kinsmen... [will long be liberated].
One has already attained equal and perfect enlightenment within the Land of Lotus; how, then, could there still be talk of "reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth"?
If this were not so, one should simply rely on the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" as a guide for the path to rebirth.
Have you not seen what the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra* says: "If a person with a sincere heart makes their voice uninterrupted, they will be fully endowed [with the merit]..."

Ten recitations: by invoking the name of Namo Amitābha Buddha, through the power of calling upon the Buddha’s name, one eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas within every single thought-moment.
At the time of death, one will see a golden lotus flower, like a sun-disk, appearing before that person.
In the space of a single thought-moment, one immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Having been reborn there, one beholds the Buddha.

Upon hearing the Dharma, one awakens to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Only then does one realize that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not some other place, and that Amitābha is not some other person.
Reaching this point, if you simply say, "One recitation of the Buddha's name," even if it makes your mouth sore for three days, what fault could there be?
Do you understand? The moment of transformation and birth upon the lotus pedestal is precisely this very thought-moment of the present.
Lin Zunru, a literatus, recommended Master Kǎoxiùxiān for a small *cán* (meditative discourse) before the spirit tablet. The Master said:
"Old layman Xiùxiān, eighty-seven years ago, from which path did you come? Eighty-seven years later, by which path will you go?
If you clearly know the place of coming and going, then what are the two characters 'birth' and 'death'?"
Ha! A mirage and a flower in the sky. If you have not yet realized this, I cannot help but expose it for you:
From where did you come eighty-seven years ago? *Dot!* To where will you go eighty-seven years after? *Dot!* Do you understand? Whether living or dying, I say nothing at all.
Avalokiteśvara manifests his entire body everywhere.
Small Sermon. The Master said: "Since Lady Chen Hanshou passed away, three years have already elapsed.

Now, as this marks the auspicious anniversary, her filial sons, Zeng Gongtiao, Wei Li, and Gongshuo, have specifically ascended Mount Gu at this time to perform repentance rites and provide a vegetarian feast for the monks."

This is offered to dedicate merit for the peace of the deceased. Furthermore, I request that this mountain monk come to the spirit to provide instruction. Listen attentively, Madam: the void is boundless;
who is east and who is west? Within the ten realms there is no person; who is ordinary and who is sage? It is solely because of a single moment of non-awakening that one perceives flowers in the air.
One rises or sinks according to the delusions of karma, and continues to be stirred by causes and conditions through many lifetimes.
The waves have not returned to this day. If you, my lady, can cast open the true eye right here, you will return home along the path;
only then will you know that the lamp is fire and the rice is food. As for Śākyamuni, what is he but a dried-up piece of excrement?
Dharma was originally but an old, hairy barbarian. What more need be said?
Regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, if you have not yet realized this, you, my lady, should first examine the phrase "prior to birth. Discern carefully whether it is male or female.
Once you personally behold his face, the flowers of the iron tree will bloom with a fragrance beyond the kalpas. Be careful!

For the sake of his Dharma friend, Chan Master Fazhen, the Master held a small *canshan* (private memorial discourse) before the spirit tablet. The Master said: "Dharma friend Fazhen, you formerly studied together with me under our late teacher.

You were extremely diligent in practicing the Way, yet you harbored a sense of self-importance regarding your own insights and looked down upon your peers. Alas, Heaven did not grant you a full lifespan;
you passed away carrying your aspirations with you. Everyone lamented this loss. Now your disciple Xingchang and your grand-disciple Fazhi have already brought forth your remains."

He entered the stupa. Now, having returned to the mountain once more, he performed prostrations and repentance to offer posthumous merit for his late master, requesting the mountain monk to preach the Dharma before the spirit to repay the kindness of his inspiration.
At this moment, tell me: was there a place where he met Fa-zhen?

If you say there was a meeting, then the realms of the unseen and the seen are utterly separated. If you say there was no meeting, then their nostrils have always been connected. Meeting or not meeting—[tell me].
Let us set aside the matter of seeing for now. As for Fa-zhen, six years have already passed since he entered the world of the dead.

Whether it be among the heavens, among humans, or within the pure lands of the Buddhas, there must be a place where he has been entrusted. But tell me: where is this single aperture within the nostrils entrusted?
Since there is no place of entrustment, there is likewise no appearing or disappearing, no movement or stillness, and no coming or going—whether a Buddha exists or not.
Its nature and characteristics are eternally abiding; it is as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as empty space.
Even so, this is still but a figurative designation. As for what Fazhen personally saw in his own time—was there not much more than that?
This single phrase must be spoken by Fazhen himself before it can be accepted. After a long silence, he said: "Assembly, do not say that Fazhen has nothing to say."
Very well. Take care.
A brief *shōsan* (private funeral discourse) for the sake of the spiritual friend Lin Changjie, before his remains. The Master said:

"The two characters 'birth' and 'death' have caused how many people to become deluded, and yet they have also caused how many people to awaken. Why do they cause so many to become deluded? It is because the worldly people lack the eye of wisdom."
Look! This cycle of birth and death remains unbroken; driven by it, one wanders through kalpa after kalpa, wave upon wave. Is this not how many have been deluded?

And why is it that so many have attained awakening? If one possesses the numinous roots planted in past lives, they will immediately see through this birth and death as utterly ungraspable. Thus attaining great sovereignty—is this not how many have awakened?
Thus we know that the two characters "birth-and-death" (saṃsāra) are truly the crux for the holy and the ordinary, the very gateway between delusion and awakening.
As for those who have awakened, birth-and-death has been emptied; ultimately, where do they go? After a long silence, he said: "Pluck out the cataract from the eye."
Return to your original face; fundamentally, there is no dwelling or attachment. A phantom guest in the precious lotus pond, Amitābha personally bestows a prediction of enlightenment.
All the sages join in supporting you to the highest grade of the highest birth. To the east or west of Zhaozhou’s courtyard—Changjie Shanyou, simply transcend and escape right here.
Buryuan’s father, Lin Tingqian, and Ru’an’s father, Chen Wudou, along with their mother, Lady He, jointly requested a small *can* (sermon) before the spirit tablets.
The Master said: "Buryuan’s father is not Ru’an’s father; Ru’an’s mother is not Buryuan’s mother.
Tonight, we enter together into the Tathāgata’s Great Treasury of Radiance, acting as host and guest to one another. We can only attain this now."
In the ancient past, there was one time; birth and death were one boundary, the sage and the ordinary person were one body, and delusion and awakening were one path.
Within this, if one seeks their differing characteristics, they are utterly unfindable. It is no different from being at ease with one’s parents.

If you can direct yourself toward this point, using the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) to seal and determine each thing, you will become the master wherever you are, and whenever you encounter conditions, you will manifest the fundamental source. Whether in the heavens, among humans, or in other directions—
In this realm, great functions flourish and arise, serving as a model for all beings. It is pure, naked, and vividly clear;
one no longer perceives even a hair’s breadth of any phenomenon that could act as an obstruction. Do you understand? Your entire body is already seated in the Palace of the Empty King;
there is no need to seek Śākyamuni on Vulture Peak.

Zen practitioner Benchu requested a small lecture (xiaocan) for the memorial of his parents. The Master said: “Benchu, throughout your parents’ lives, they never heard of the Dharma of non-arising (anutpāda-dharma).
You have specifically requested that this mountain monk reveal the Dharma of non-arising to you. If we discuss the Dharma of non-arising, your parents have never died;
this is because death is an illusory death. If one seeks the mark of death, it is utterly unobtainable. Benchu, as for their birth...”
That which has arisen is an illusory arising. If one seeks its characteristic of arising, it is utterly unobtainable.

This state of unobtainability is precisely the original source-nature of the person. It is only because, since beginningless kalpas, it has been covered over by the characteristics of arising and ceasing that it cannot manifest before us.
If, at this very moment, one can directly awaken to the non-existence [of self] within this unobtainability of birth and death—
When the patience regarding the arising of phenomena (*utpatti-dharma-kṣānti*) is realized, one beholds the essence as perfectly luminous, forever free from obstruction. Can you still believe this?
Once the principle of non-arising is awakened to, all conditions become utterly still. Where do the drifting clouds disperse? The bright moon is precisely in the sky.
Chen Huisheng, a virtuous friend, escorted the laywoman Daogang into her stupa and requested a small *can* (sermon) for the deceased. The Master said:
"Laywoman Daogang, you have received my Mahāyāna Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Precepts and have already entered the rank of all Buddhas.
Do you know this? Since you passed away, half a year has already elapsed. Try to observe this clearly for yourself. He finished speaking.
In the end, is there a world to which one can pay homage? Or is there no world to which one can pay homage? One must know that the world does not exist;

how then could there be a world to which one could pay homage? Yet the world is not non-existent; how then could there be no world to which one could pay homage? What are the three realms and the six paths of existence?
They are all manifestations of one’s own mind, like flowers in the sky—appearing to exist but lacking reality. Fundamentally, they cannot be reckoned as either existent or non-existent. If...
If one can, amidst the incalculable, recognize the original source-ground of the mind, then the birth and death of the three realms will instantly and suddenly become empty;
the pure precepts of the three aggregates will be fully possessed in a single thought-moment.

To shatter ignorance across vast kalpas and to transcend the Buddha-fruit over many lifetimes—all this is the constant nature of one's own mind, requiring no recourse to external arts. Do you understand yet? The nature-precepts are nothing other than this.

Nor is there any such thing; it remains unchanging from antiquity to the present. When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts for a single thought-moment, they transcend directly and enter the stage of the Tathāgata.

The Venerable Fanxi sent Master Yinxian to be enshrined in a stupa and requested a small-scale discourse (*xiaocan*). The Master said: "The debt of gratitude between teacher and disciple is profound."

"From the hills and mountains, white bones are brought to be enshrined here in this stupa. I specifically request the mountain monk to propagate the Dharma-gift, so that you may immediately enter the profound barrier.
[The Master] raises his whisk and says: "Venerable Yinxian, do you see? Once seen, it is not seen again.
He strikes the desk and says: "Do you hear? Once heard, it is not heard again. "Do you know? Once known, it is not known again. "What is it?"
The Dharma does not see the Dharma; the Dharma does not hear the Dharma; the Dharma does not know the Dharma. Do you understand this thoroughly?
The Buddha Hall faces the three gates for all time; the four great Vajras gaze together with their eyes.
Master Fanxi was invited by his uncle’s senior, Shideng, to give a small discourse (*xiaocan*). The Master said: "For over sixty years, it has been but a single dream;
now awake, the sky is already breaking into dawn. Having clearly seen my own native field, I whip up the clay ox to plow amidst the flames.
As for this native field of one's own—how is it seen? Does the Venerable Shideng know?"

Seeing and not seeing split empty space into two parts; from birth to death, it is fundamentally complete. How could there ever be front or back here? *Dot!* This was the small assembly instruction for the Lantern Festival.
The Master said: "Last night was the eve of the year’s end. The Chief Administrator, Master Mai, requested that I provide an exposition for the great assembly."

This mountain monk shall open a Dharma gate of ten points: First, one must possess a sense of shame and remorse; for those who lack shame and remorse are loathed by both humans and spirits. Second, one must recognize the Buddha’s kindness;

for those who betray his grace and fail their debt are not disciples of the Buddha. Third, one must contemplate the suffering of birth and death; for one must know weariness with and seek detachment from it.
Fourth, one must give rise to the mind that transcends the world; for one must not be attached to the three realms. Fifth, one must have deep faith.
1. Cause and effect: because the retribution of karma is never lost. 2. One must firmly uphold the precepts: because they are the root of attaining Buddhahood. 3.
One must practice Chan meditation and recite the Buddha’s name: to clearly perceive one's own nature and personally attend upon all Buddhas. 4. One must recite sutras and study:
to broaden one's knowledge and vision, thereby making one's realization perfectly integrated. 5. One must establish a system of practice: so that merit and wisdom may mutually support one another.
Tenth, one must have vast power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*), for whatever is willed shall surely be accomplished. Let the great assembly try to examine themselves:
among these ten phrases, do you possess them all or not? If you lack them entirely, you are merely a shaven-headed commoner, not a renunciant.
Such as these are not of my kind; it would be better for you to leave quickly through the three gates. Today is the Yuanxiao Festival.
The Abbot, Master Chun, further requested this mountain monk to provide an instruction for the assembly. An ancient worthy said:
"If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season. When the time and season arrive, its principle will manifest of itself.

Unable to avoid responding to the present moment and the occasion, I shall cite an ancient story for the assembly. Formerly, a monk asked Jingqing: "Is there still a Buddha at the beginning of the new year?"
The monk asked, "Is there any Dharma? Qing said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma for the beginning of the new year? Qing said, "The first day of the new year opens a new era.
The monk stepped forward and said, "Thank you, Master, for your answer. Qing said, "Today the mountain monk has lost face. Gushan said, "Two humpbacked camels have met;
to this day, there has been no upright person in the world. Furthermore, a monk asked about Mingjiao’s "New [Year]..."
At the beginning of the year, [the Master] said, "Furthermore, there is no Buddha-dharma. The monk asked, "The teaching says 'no. Why is there none?
The Master replied, "When Old Zhang drinks wine, Old Li gets drunk. The monk said, "How can you, so old and venerable, leave the dragon's head and end with the snake's tail?
The Master replied, "Today the mountain monk has suffered a loss. Gushan said, "Jade is naturally without flaw; carving patterns destroys its virtue."
Today, someone asked Gushan, "At the beginning of the New Year, is there still any Buddha-dharma? He replied, "The Buddha-dharma is not here.
When further asked where it is, he said to him, "By day it is hot as fire; at evening the wind roars like thunder.
If the person says, "Thank you for your answer," Gushan gives him a cup of tea. If he says, "Old man..."
Great man! To begin with vigor but end with weakness—Drum Mountain shall also give him a cup of tea. Why is this so?
Because rewards and punishments must be clear and distinct. Take care.
The Master gave a small-scale sermon for the attendants. He said, "In the monastic community, every hundred duties has its appointed office;
we rely solely upon the great-minded monks to maintain sincerity together, each extending a hand: those who cook rice cook rice, and those who brew tea brew tea."
Those who burn incense burn incense; those who sweep the floor sweep the floor.
They welcome and guide future practitioners so that, in their eyes, ears, noses, and tongues, each faculty is fully complete without lack, and each is thoroughly penetrating without obstruction.
This is indeed the fundamental style of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and it is also the ordinary conduct of Zen monks. Only...
It is like Kātyāyana in the hall: what was he teaching others? For many years he sat in meditation, observing only his nose;
no matter who came, he would not raise his head.
When Chan Master Daozun was offering incense for the memorial of his late mother, Lady Zhou, he requested a small *shanchan* (sermon before the spirit). The Master said: "The Provincial Governor..."
The Grain Transport Commissioner of the Provincial Administration, Mr.

Chen Tai-sun, leading his assembly of filial descendants, ascended specifically to Mount Gu to perform rites of repentance and provide a vegetarian feast for monks, in order to dedicate merit for the posthumous benefit of his late mother, Lady Zhou Taigongren.
He further commanded the mountain monk to go to her memorial site to expound upon the principles of birth and death. Does Lady Taigongren still know? If birth were truly real, how...
There is death; since there is death, birth is non-birth. If death were real, how could there be birth?
Since there is birth, death is non-death. Where there is no birth and no death, the adamantine true essence is manifest and majestic.
To seek its arising and ceasing within this state is like planting rabbit horns on a horse’s head or scraping tortoise hair from a snake’s back.
How could such a thing be? Take, for instance, Lady Taigong:

right now, sustained by the Buddha’s radiance, she is fully manifest, vividly and uniquely luminous—she who listens to this mountain monk preaching the Dharma. Tell me, what is she? After a long silence, he said:
"In the past, Jianyuan attended Daowu. When they went to a donor’s house to offer condolences, Jianyuan placed his hand on the coffin and asked, 'Is she alive?'"
"Is it death? Wuye said, "I do not say 'life,' nor do I say 'death. Yuansheng asked, "Why do you not speak? Wuye replied, "I do not speak;
I do not speak. Yuansheng did not understand. One day, he heard a youth reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra:
"If one should be saved by means of a bhikṣu’s body, he immediately manifests in the form of a bhikṣu. At that moment, he attained great enlightenment. Master Taigong understood this in full detail.
"Ma! I will say nothing of birth; I will say nothing of death. At midnight, the stone man has no shadow or image;
how can one distinguish between the source and the destination, however they may appear? To those who should be saved by the body of a bhikṣu, he manifests as a bhikṣu.
When the dragon roars, mist rises; when the tiger howls, the wind arises. But as for that manifested body—appearing and disappearing, hidden and revealed—is there still birth and death? Thereupon...
[The Master] said: "I do not say it; I do not say it. I humbly entreat you to take care of yourself.
This is the literary man Chen Zidu, who, on behalf of his late mother, Lady Zhang, requests a small *śamaya* (private discourse) before the spirit.
The Master said: "Today, the filial son Chen Kai has been mourning for his late mother, Lady Zhang, for seven years since she passed away. Every..."
Deeply cherishing the compassion of her upbringing, he was moved by the poignant sentiment of the "wind and wood" (the filial longing for one's parents).

Realizing that no power but the Buddha’s could repay his mother’s kindness, he ascended specifically to Mount Gu, invoking the spiritual presence of the Great Compassionate One and devoting his heart to the methods of repentance, thereby cleansing his past transgressions.
To plant the seeds of auspicious fortune for the future—O Venerable Lady, you must know that this fortune is not obtained from without; it originates from the mind.
Since the mind is unborn, fortune is likewise unconditioned. If one realizes the essence of the unborn mind, then in every place and at all times, [fortune will manifest].
Constantly turning the fundamental wheel of Dharma, in every land and within every atom of dust, he fully reveals the *amala* consciousness as the ground of the mind.
Although he dwells among the heavens like the heavens, he cannot be encompassed by them; though he dwells among men like men, he cannot be contained by them.
Thus it is said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast. It can act as the lord of all things, yet does not follow the four seasons."
Withered. Does the respectful lady still know? From immeasurable kalpas, it has always been thus; not a single hair’s breadth has ever been shifted.
When one realizes this within the conditions, all doubts are exhausted; only then does one see that from the beginning, one has stood tall.
Wang Chuanshi offered a memorial service for the abbot Huiyun and requested a *xiaocan* (small formal sermon) on his behalf. The Master said:

"The female disciple Wang Chuanshi has observed the vow of chastity since childhood and is now already white-haired. For a long time she has relied upon the abbot Huiyun to diligently cultivate the Pure Land practices.
Now that the abbot has passed away, I am overcome with grief and lamentation. I have therefore specially contributed funds to perform rites of repentance as a meritorious offering for him."
I have again requested this mountain monk to preach the Dharma before the spirit to repay the debt of gratitude for the Dharma. Does Master Huiyun of An know?
Among the sentient beings of the three realms, there are none who are not constrained by birth and death. This birth and death is not obtained from without.
It is created by one's own mind. Thus Vajragarbha said: "Birth and death are both created by the mind;
if the mind is extinguished, birth and death are exhausted. But as for this mind—how is it to be extinguished? The past mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended;
the present mind cannot be apprehended. The past has already ceased; the future has not yet arrived; the present is empty and quiescent.
In this way, the mind itself cannot be apprehended. What, then, can be called birth and death? Since birth and death are empty, nirvana is likewise quiescent. Therefore it is said:
"Seeking the mind throughout the three periods of time, the mind is not found; where the mind is not found, delusion is fundamentally non-existent;
where delusion is fundamentally non-existent, that is bodhi. Birth and death and nirvana are fundamentally equal. Within this dharma of equality, there is no present.

There is no past. There is neither awakening nor delusion; there is neither male nor female; there is neither sin nor merit. Whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature and characteristics remain eternally as they are.

Master Huiyun, you must here and now cast off your burden and return home; only then will you shift your position to meet the pivot, so that clarity shines upon every point and manifestation appears in every thing.
You shall cultivate the Buddhist rites of empty flowers and establish a Dharma assembly of the moon reflected in water.

Prostrate before the demonic armies within the mirror; realize the fruit of Buddhahood amidst a dream. Although it is thus, there remains one phrase where both function and stage are utterly extinguished;
wait for our meeting on another day, and I shall break it open for you once more.
Small Lecture on the Mid-Autumn Festival. The Master said: "Tonight, the golden wind fans the wilds and the full moon flows with radiance.
A light drizzle wets the empty steps; vast, thin clouds drift across the autumn Milky Way. At such a time as this, tell me: whose affair is this?
You must know that each person possesses a piece of secure and secret ground, yet for many years it has been cast aside amidst the weeds."
The inner lining. Now, such a favorable opportunity is difficult to encounter. I have plucked this out with my own hand; those with eyes must take care not to see it.
It is permitted only for those without a mind to know. Even so, thirty years hence, do not say that Gushan used the property of the monastery as a personal favor.
For the late Senior Monk Guangxuan, on behalf of his son, the scholar Shao Zixian, an invitation was requested for a small *can* (meditative discourse) before the spirit tablet. The Master said:

"Zixian, you must remain alert and aware. Today, your honorable father, Senior Monk Guangxuan, unable to overcome his grief and lamentation over your death at the hands of bandits, has specially offered his robes and bowl as an act of repentance and merit for your posthumous advancement. He has further requested this mountain monk to come to your side."
I preach the Dharma to guide and instruct you; do you still understand? Zilu tied his sash before death, while Zeng Shen changed his mat at the end;

though they both emerged from the gate of the Sage, their karmic results were vastly different. Now, although the two words "cause and effect" were spoken by the Buddha, the school of Confucius has likewise never denied cause and effect.

The *Great Changes* (*Yijing*) speaks of "accumulating goodness brings remaining blessings" and "accumulating non-goodness brings remaining calamity," which corresponds to the five blessings and six extremes of the *Book of Documents* (*Hongfan*).
All of these are doctrines concerning cause and effect. Nevertheless, as Sima Qian once said: "The Way of Heaven has no partiality; it always favors the virtuous.
Now, were Bo Yi and Shu Qi not to be called virtuous men? Yet despite their accumulation of benevolence and purity of conduct, they died of hunger.
Furthermore, among the seventy disciples, Confucius alone recommended Yan Yuan for his love of learning. Yet even he was short-lived. How can this be reconciled with the doctrine of retribution?
Yet Hui was frequently destitute; he never grew weary of eating dregs and coarse grain, yet in the end he died young. How, then, did Heaven reward such a virtuous man?
As for Robber Zhi, he killed the innocent every day and ate human liver;

he was violent and tyrannical, gathering a band of several thousand men to roam across the world at will, yet he lived out his full span of life. By what virtue did he follow? These cases are most clearly manifest.

This is clearly evident. Yet, if we look at recent times, there are those whose conduct is unprincipled and who specialize in violating taboos, yet they enjoy pleasure and merriment for their entire lives, and their wealth and prosperity continue for generations without end.

Conversely, there are those who choose their steps with care, speak only when the time is right, do not take bypaths, and exert themselves only for what is just—yet those who meet with calamity and disaster are beyond counting. I...
I am greatly perplexed. Is what is called the Way of Heaven thus, or not? This is because the Sima clan suspects that good and evil leave no trace and that cause and effect are in disorder;
yet they fail to realize that our Buddha taught that karmic retribution spans three periods of time: the first is retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).

This refers to three types of retribution: first, immediate retribution, which means that good or evil deeds performed in the present life yield results in this very life; second, retribution in the next life, which means the results begin to manifest after one has passed through one birth;
and third, subsequent retribution, which means the results only manifest after many lifetimes have elapsed. Ordinary people do not understand this principle of the three types of retribution;

seeing only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious meet with fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune, they hastily claim that cause and effect do not exist and that merit and retribution are empty.
Little do you realize that [karma] follows form like a shadow, without the slightest deviation; even after passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it shall never perish.
Now, you, Master Xian, are a man of talent and virtue, a gentleman of literary refinement and conduct, possessing a brilliant intellect and a wondrous nature.

That you have suddenly met an untimely death cannot help but cause you the same confusion as that of Sima Qian. If you understand the doctrine of the three retributions, then your doubts will surely dissolve like ice melting away.
Although this is so, one must further understand that retribution arises from the stirring of karma, and karma is created by the mind. The mind is fundamentally unborn;

all things are like illusions. If one can awaken to and enter the essence of the unborn mind, then all karmic obstructions, retributive obstructions, and afflictive obstructions will be purified simultaneously.
Whether in other realms or this world, whether in the heavens or among humans, one dwells according to conditions without any lingering attachment.
Obstruction. As for this single phrase of "entering through awakening," how is it? "From the crown of the head, he releases the eye of Mahesvara;
it shines through the three thousandfold world and the great chiliocosm. Take care.
The disciples, including Gui and others, requested that the Master provide a small discourse (*xiaocan*) for their teacher, Master Dezhi. The Master said: "Obscured is the original non-existence;
flowers in the void bloom in confusion. The body that comes and goes through birth and death—how could its cycle ever have an end?
Nevertheless, when there is movement, move; when there is stillness, rest. A lamp is fire; rice is grain. Do you know this yet? Come now."
"Listen to this mountain monk’s Dharma talk. Is it not you yourself—those who cannot attain life when seeking it, nor attain death when seeking it?
*Tut!* For the sake of the late father Zheng Gongyu, son Zheng Jing and others request this informal discourse before the spirit. The Master says: *Yusheng*."
"Old Layman, today your sons, Zheng Jingyu, Zheng Ding, and others, have specifically ascended Mount Gu for you, the Old Layman, to offer prayers for your posthumous merit.
They have further requested that I, this mountain monk, go to the spirit’s abode to preach the Dharma. As the Patriarch Aśvaghoṣa said:
'The Dharma refers to the mind of sentient beings. You must know that this mind gives rise to heaven and earth, gives rise to humans, and gives rise to the myriad things—and yet this mind..."

There has never been anything born; it is like being driven about in a dream while the body remains fundamentally unmoving. Space encompasses all phenomena, yet space itself is fundamentally unconditioned.

If one realizes this unborn essence of mind, then upon the path of birth and death, one proceeds directly forward and comes directly back, seeing not even so much as a single hair’s breadth of any phenomenon that could act as an obstruction or hindrance.
Why is this? Because when the true eye is opened wide, it is no longer a dream-state.
Because it can be deluded and confused. At such a time, does the old layman still know where he stands? The single nature is perfectly luminous, beyond gain or loss;
awakening through conditions does not depend on another. On the road of birth and death there is no path of birth;
within the fire blooms the utpala flower.
Filial Daughter Guo Shuzhen, performing the Blood Basin Repentance Rite, requests that a verse be spoken. The Master says: "In days of yore, Mulian once initiated this teaching;

through the Lanpen rite, he enabled his mother to be reborn in heaven. Now, specifically following these bequeathed tracks, the pure fast is completed; I pray that both parents may be recommended to reach the Nine Lotuses."
The disciple Jie Ru respectfully requests that the Master Hongru Yang be invited to preside over his entry into the stupa and to deliver a small discourse (*xiaocan*).
The Master said: "To be at home is to be a father; to leave the home-life is to be a teacher. Whether in the mundane world or the world-transcending realm, the Way is subtle and profound.
It is like this: once the fire has achieved its work, it is carried to the summit of Shigushan. But for what purpose? To sit and cut off the paths to the north and south of Xiangnan and Tantan."
Upon the lotus pedestal, another son was born.

His filial sons, Hwang Ji-hong and Ji-kwon, offered this memorial service for their deceased parents and requested a small discourse (so-sam). The Master said: "Life and death are like bubbles upon the water;
Rising and ceasing with the wind, they flow on without pause. Through conditions, one realizes the principle of non-birth; The ocean of nature..."
What prevents you from playing and wandering about? As for the principle of non-arising, how will you realize it? Vajrapāṇi stares with bared fangs, ever facing [the world];
Maitreya laughs "he-he" without ceasing.
Small Precept Assembly on the Mid-Autumn Festival. The Master said: "Last night the moon was waning yet bright; tonight the moon is full yet dark.
How many people have gazed upon it, each giving rise to sighs and lamentations! But tell me, is there still waxing and waning within the Palace of Cold Radiance?"
Furthermore, there is neither light nor darkness; there is neither joy nor sorrow. Arriving here, even if one were to say:
"The toad lacks the power of reflection; the jade hare lacks the intent to accompany the moon; even the sovereigns Yao and Shun still have their transformative influence remaining."

"As for that single phrase which does not fall into the gate of transformation—how is it? The assembly, having finished drinking tea, shall return to the hall for a small session of instruction (*xiao-can*).
In the hall, the Master said: 'Just now Gu-biao asked me, "What is the place where one applies the mind when practicing Zen?"'"
The mountain monk answered him, saying: "If you resolve to practice for the sake of birth and death, you will naturally know how to apply the mind;

if you do not resolve to practice for the sake of birth and death, you will not know how to apply the mind. He asked again, "What is the point at which practicing Chan becomes effective? The mountain monk said:
"If you apply effort for the sake of birth and death, you will gain effectiveness; if you do not apply effort for the sake of birth and death, you will not gain effectiveness."
He asked again, "What is the eye that penetrates the barrier? The mountain monk replied, "I will tell you once you have penetrated the barrier.
The man refused to accept this and did not prostrate; he simply shook his sleeves and returned to the assembly. The mountain monk then struck him severely.
"Tell me, the assembly," he said, "when I answered thus and struck him thus, was there any room for benefiting others? If you say there was..."
If you say there is a place for people, you have failed the ancient standard. If you say there is no place for people, you have likewise failed this mountain monk.
If anyone can reach a definitive conclusion regarding this point, I grant that they possess the true eye. Otherwise, let me provide another analogy for you.
What is the place where one applies the mind in Zen practice? It is like a person walking on a road, never stopping for a single step.
What is the place where one gains power in Zen practice? It is like a person walking on a road, reaching home at every step. What is the eye that penetrates the barrier?
No matter how many thousands or tens of thousands of people try to ensnare it, they cannot hold it back; simply look in this way.
Lingshi Huansheng and Dishimoxue addressed the assembly of precept-holders, requesting a small-scale discourse (*xiaocan*) on behalf of their teacher’s birthday celebration.
The Master said: "If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of themselves. What is this 'eye that does not sleep'? It is the state where antiquity and the present are never obscured.
If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are as they are. What is this 'mind that does not differ'? It is the profound spirit that transcends all dependence. With such an eye..."
Contemplate such a mind as the merging of space with space, or like a mirror reflecting a mirror.
If you perceive even so much as a hair-tip’s worth of the signs of arising and ceasing, it is but a dream. But what of it when the bright mirror is smashed to pieces and empty space is rent asunder?
The cold plum tree has captured the news of spring; amidst the snow, its branches lean and twist as they compete to burst forth in bloom.
To the Dharma-friend Lin Danzhang: Having gathered funds for the collection and interment of remains, you have requested a small *can* (sermon) before the spirits. The Master said:

"Virtuous son Lin Danzhang, you have mobilized the masses to collect and bury ownerless skulls throughout the four suburbs of Fucheng, totaling one thousand eight hundred and more individuals, both male and female.
Upon completion of these tasks, you have further ascended to Gushan to perform great Buddhist rites for their benefit and to dedicate merit to your own [ancestors]."

May the deceased members of the family, the ancestors of the lineage, and all kinsmen equally partake in this merit for their peace in the afterlife. Furthermore, I request that the mountain monk preach the Dharma before the spirit.
May all spirits be clearly aware: as for this very skull—is it you, or is it not you?
If it is you, why is it devoid of knowledge and consciousness while being scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind? If it is not you, then where is that single spark of conscious spirit? Why...

They remain deeply attached and do not relinquish it. Do you still understand? It is because of the root of delusion from beginningless time that, within a mind and body that have no inherent existence, one falsely clings to the appearances of body and mind.
The body so clung to belongs to the four great elements, while the mind that clings belongs to the six sense objects.

Contemplate the body by detaching it from the four great elements; it is like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. Contemplate the mind by detaching it from the six sense objects; it resembles a mirage or flowers in the sky.
When the true eye is opened wide at this point, you will personally behold your original face.
Not even a single speck of dust can be found; what, then, could be called "body and mind" or "birth and death"? Therefore it is said: "Clearly seeing, there is not a single thing. Nor...
There is no person and no thing. The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean; all worthies and sages are like a flash of lightning.

Although there is not a single thing, you who are now riding upon the Buddha’s compassionate light and attending this Dharma assembly—this distinct, solitary luminosity that hears the mountain monk preach the Dharma—is what, pray tell? *Dot!* What else could it be? Take care!
New Year’s Eve Small Sermon: We who are here beneath this *kāṣāya* robe enjoy the protective shade of the Buddha.

We are free from the burdens of parents and wives, and untainted by the disturbances of official duties or private debts. Our food and clothing are provided for; a hundred concerns do not enter our thoughts.
Thus we pass the year—its three hundred and sixty days—unaware and unknowing. If there is not a single piece of genuine reality here, [all is in vain].
To accomplish the work of the Path with body and mind and establish true practice—how could this be done in a single year?
I fear that even in an entire lifetime, one may pass away in just this manner. Would this not be to deceive and mislead oneself, and to fail the Buddha’s kindness?

Therefore, when the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he earnestly offered this admonition: "One should constantly reflect that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds; seek [liberation] for yourself early."
"O you who have crossed over! If we are truly able to contemplate impermanence and seek our own deliverance from birth and death, what need is there to speak of delivering sentient beings?
Does the great assembly still understand impermanence?"

Small Sermon for the Lantern Festival: In the heavens, a single orb of moon; Upon the earth, ten thousand households of lanterns. The pure light merges into one expanse; Auspicious vapors rise in profusion.
Do not take this as an encounter with external objects; Do not take this as an encounter with the mind; Do not take this as an encounter where both object and mind are forgotten.
Ultimately, how is it? "I behold the Lamp-Bright Buddha; His fundamental radiance is thus auspicious."

The filial son Zhang Huiguang, a Taizhong official, offered a memorial for his deceased mother and requested a small discourse before her spirit. The Master said: "All dharmas arise through the convergence of conditions.

Since they arise through the convergence of conditions, that which has not yet arisen does not exist; when conditions disperse, they perish. If they were to exist as substantial realities, then once existing, they could never perish.
Only the fundamental enlightened nature inherent in each person is not produced by causes and conditions; how could it have arisen?"
To extinguish it is to cause confusion; it is simply a matter of valuing that single thought-moment of turning the faculty of mind.

If you see directly, then once this is clearly seen, the two words "birth and death" are themselves the eternally abiding ocean of great quiescent extinction. What more can be said of birth and death?
It is just like the laywoman Dayou, who now, receiving the Buddha’s radiance, comes to hear this mountain monk preach the Dharma. This—
These points are distinct and solitary luminosity. Is there birth and death? Is there delusion and awakening?
There is no need for this mountain monk to provide further pointers; it is best that you investigate and contemplate this for yourself.
The senior master Hongneng, Xuejing, and his disciple [the deceased] Zhaosheng—whose father was Huang Wenxiu and mother Wang;
and Zhaoxuan—whose father was Wu Yongnian and mother Luo—are jointly making this offering. We request a small discourse before the spirit. The Master said:
"From birth to death, the essence is fundamentally complete; within this, how could there ever be any separation? Today, because of the wind, a single thread is passed through. The mud ox..."
"Treading through the sky within the water. After treading through it, what then? "Brother Hongneng has transcended the ultimate reality;
he has elevated his parents to the precious lotus.

For the funeral service of Master Chuyun, who offered incense for his parents, the Master was requested to deliver a small *can* (sermon) before the spirit. The Master said: "Master Chuyun lost his mother at the age of six..."
The parents are currently over fifty years of age, yet their longing for one another has not diminished.

Today, they have specifically donated their robes and bowls to provide a meal for the monastics at Drum Mountain (Gushan) in order to dedicate merit for their peace in the afterlife. They further request that I, this mountain monk, go to their spirits to preach the Dharma.
Parents Chuyun, you must know that the Dharma is fundamentally without form, for it is not an object of the mind, intellect, or consciousness; the Dharma is fundamentally beyond words.
Because the path of language is cut off, dharmas are without arising or ceasing. Because birth and death cannot defile them, dharmas have no limit.
Because they cannot be measured by worldly quantities, they are beyond calculation. Indeed, the self is itself the dharma, and the dharma is itself the self.
There is nothing to be said in speaking, and nothing to be heard in hearing. Thus, throughout vast eons, through birth after birth and death after death...
Life after life, like a whirling firebrand, there is no rest. What, ultimately, is this? A mirage, flowers in the sky—do you understand this thoroughly?
Father and son are naturally and truly in sublime accord; when one phrase is fully brought forth, past and present are extinguished.
The filial son Lin Taiding, on behalf of his late father, Layman Wenruo, requested a small-scale formal discourse (xiaochan) before the spirit tablet.
The Master said: "All Buddhas attain liberation through the mind; the mind is pure and is named 'stainless. It is fresh and clean within the five realms of existence, remaining unstained.
Those who understand this realize the Way. As for the sentient beings of the three realms, their comings and goings in birth and death are chaotic and confused—how can this be?"
One must understand the principle of being pure and untainted. Take, for example, the layman Lin Gongwenruo:
he came fifty-nine years ago and will depart fifty-nine years hence;

yet during those very fifty-nine years in between, he managed his household affairs, served his parents with filial piety, and educated his children, tirelessly seeking merit through the practice of goodness without turning back. Now tell me: was he stained or was he unstained?
"This is understanding; this is non-understanding. If you say that non-understanding is defilement and understanding is non-defilement, this is a view of arising and ceasing;
it has not yet transcended ordinary sentiment. You must know that it is like a *maṇi* jewel, which reflects all five colors in its perfect luminosity.

If you say it is defiled, it is transparent through and through; if you say it is undefiled, it is brilliantly manifest. If you can recognize the substance of the jewel, then as for understanding and non-understanding—
[The Master] said: "To speak of 'defiled' and 'undefiled' is all superfluous talk. At this very moment, tell me: where is the pearl? After a long silence, he said:
"A single perfect sphere, without interior or exterior; Shining through the present and illuminating the past, it transcends the subtle and the minute.
The Buddhas of the three ages do not know its existence; It is granted only to the dark-skinned ox to know it alone."
The filial son, King He, offers this memorial service for his late mother, Lady Xie, and requests a small *canshan* (private discourse) before her spirit. The Master said:

"The teachings state that within the pure realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is not a single thing that ever exists once it has been extinguished. Yet, by following conditions of defilement or purity, it gives rise to the ten dharma-realms.
Thus, delusion and awakening, sages and ordinary beings, coming and going, and birth and death are like dreams, like illusions, like shadows, and like echoes. Why is this so?"
Regarding phenomena born of conditions: if one says they exist, their nature is ultimately empty; if one says they do not exist, they manifest with brilliant clarity.
Existence cannot be found, nor can non-existence; increase cannot be found, nor can decrease. Within this state of unobtainability lies the single true Dharma-realm.
Standing forth alone and revealed, what further room is there for talk of delusion and enlightenment, sages and ordinary beings, coming and going, or birth and death?
Yongjia said: "Clearly seeing that not a single thing exists, there is neither person nor Buddha;
the great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the sea, and all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning. Striking the whisk, he said: "Lady Xie, simply turn toward this very place. Directly!
"Returning to the source below. Take care.
The laywoman Zhang offered this memorial for her deceased husband and requested a small-scale sermon (xiaocan) before his spirit. The Master said:
"Xie Junji and I, along with my late son Xinjian, have been gone from this world for three years now. As days pass and months shift, the illusion of the four elements [of the body]..."

The body does not abide. With parents aged and a wife and children young, the affection of a lifetime is difficult to relinquish. Since the eye of wisdom has not yet opened, by what means can one transcend and be liberated?
His filial wife, Lady Zhang, entered Baoshan Monastery specifically to perform repentance rites, feed the Sangha, and carry out various Buddhist services to support his merit in the afterlife.

She further requested that I, a mountain monk, go to the spirit’s resting place to preach the Dharma. As it is said in the scriptures: "There has never been a single dharma that did not arise from..."
Because they arise through causes and conditions, there is not a single dharma that is not empty.
Thus, birth is empty, and death is empty; even to speak of "neither birth nor death" is itself empty.
You must know that this emptiness is the vast source of the thousand sages and the fundamental root of the myriad spirits. For immeasurable kalpas, we, father and son, have been entangled within it.
Life and death—simply turn toward this very point and attain liberation directly. Take care.
Venerable Xuánwén was requested to deliver a small *cān* (sermon) for the spirit of his master, Zhībái. The Master said:
"Zhībái Xuán, you followed your son into the monastic life and accomplished pure practice. This year you are eighty-two years old; you have chanted the Buddha’s name until the appointed time."

He passed away while seated; the evidence of his rebirth in the West is clear. Today, his son, Taiyin, has specifically come to Gushan to provide a meal for the monks and perform memorial rites, requesting this mountain monk to preach the Dharma before the spirit to assist him in attaining rebirth. Do you understand?

The Western Land is right before one's eyes, and Amitābha is originally oneself. It is only because you have recited "The Great Man" (Shang Daren) too often that, at the end, it naturally... [is obscured].

"You may know the ritual. But when you have realized it, what then? When one is born by transformation upon the lotus pedestal, one receives the personal prediction of enlightenment before the emerald steps.

By the filial son Xue Yudong, this is respectfully offered in dedication to his late father, the Grand Master of the Middle Grade (Dazhong Dafu), Censor-in-Chief of the Shandong Provincial Administration Commission."
At the request of Layman Ruoyuan of Xuezheng, the Master held a small *śāmaṇa* (sermon) before his spirit. The Master said: "Alas, Great Layman Ruoyuan!
Have you departed so suddenly? Yet there is one who does not depart. I recall your visit to me in the mountains last spring;

although I had not yet fully poured forth my inner depths for you, you had already witnessed the presence of the Way with your own eyes. When winter arrived, I suddenly heard the news that you had laid down your mat."
The multitude all sighed with admiration and lamented [his departure]. Only the mountain monk and the layman remained silent, forgetting each other beyond words. Why?
When the layman was in his prime, he attained the highest degree, entered the literary academies, presided over the examination halls, and served extensively in various external offices;
his administration was renowned for its integrity, and everyone considered him successful. But what, indeed, did the layman attain? If there were anything attained, then at this very moment—
In what place does one abide? Once the conditions of this world have come to an end, one suddenly and completely abandons kin, retinue, and official rank, departing forever with a light step.
Everyone considers this a loss; yet as for the lay practitioner (*gṛhapati*), what is there to lose?

If there were something lost, then who is it that comes and goes, entering and exiting between heaven and the human realm? This vivid, solitary luminosity right before you—listen as the mountain monk strikes [the gong].
This is a tangle. And what, moreover, is it? Therefore, those who attain it are like floating clouds arising in the great void;
those who lose it are like floating bubbles dispersing upon the vast ocean. Though the bubbles disperse, the vast ocean remains serene; though the clouds arise at will, the long sky remains unmoving.
This state of serenity and immovability—sentient beings are deluded by it, and it becomes the cycle of birth and death within the six realms. Bodhi...
When cultivated by sentient beings, it constitutes the six perfections and myriad practices; when realized by the Buddhas, it becomes unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore it is said: "To be deluded by it is the beginning of birth and death; to awaken to it is the cessation of saṃsāra. Thus, delusion and awakening reside in the person, not in the Dharma.
Weak and aged lay brother, if you were to directly accept this right here, you would transcend birth and death at once.
But as for that single phrase of "accepting"—how is it? A former Buddha, the World-Honored One, said: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure;

from the beginning, there is neither birth nor anything to be extinguished. This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit. To dwell thus—
Gentlemen, simply realize it in this way. I humbly entreat you to take care of yourselves.
Your filial son, Zhao Menghou, Mengzhi, and Mengzhi, offer this memorial service for his late father, Layman Yuan'an, and request a small discourse before the spirit.
The Master said: "Does the Layman Yuan know? One receives a body through the convergence of three conditions, yet this body is not 'mine.
As years and months pass, one calculates one's lifespan, yet that lifespan does not increase for me. From the moment we first fell to the ground, every thought-moment has shifted in secret;
it is ever-new and never abides. Even if one were to live for a hundred years, a thousand years, ten thousand years, or even eighty-four thousand years..."
In the end, all returns to extinction. This is because worldly people do not recognize the Real; they take the delusory to be real. They do not recognize the delusory;
they are confused about the Real and take it to be delusory. The True Body is formless, pervading and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm. The True Life-span does not undergo transition.

It abides eternally throughout billions of kalpas. Because one does not know this, one stumbles through the six realms of existence, wandering back and forth between birth and death like a whirling firebrand, without rest. Therefore, the Elder Śākyamuni said:

"The continuous succession of birth and death for all sentient beings arises entirely from their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind, the nature of pure clarity; instead, they employ various false conceptions. This...

Perceptions are not real; therefore, there is cyclic existence. Right now, shatter the false and return to the true—this single phrase for suddenly transcending birth and death—how can one express it?
"The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
Layman Yuanyuan, simply realize it in this way.
The disciples Wensheng and Wen gui offered the recommendation for Master Shaoxin to give a small *can* (private instruction) before the spirit.
The Master said: "Seven days have passed since the passing of Elder Shaoxin. Now tell me: was it Shaoxin before the seven days?
Was it Shaoxin after the seven days? Or was it Shaoxin exactly at the seven-day mark? If [it were] before the seven days..."
It is so. What is there that dies? If it were so after seven days, what is there that is born? Since neither the preceding nor the succeeding [moments] exist, how could the middle be real?
Therefore it is said: "The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.
Within this state of non-apprehensibility, sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death; likewise, the Buddhas abide within this non-apprehensibility.
Attaining the Middle Way is the direct realization of Bodhi. Although delusion and awakening differ, they both ultimately return to non-attainment.
This state of non-attainment is where you establish your body and sustain your life. Do you know? One cycle of birth and death is but a single dream;
from beginningless time until now, you have still not awakened. Today, when the skull is shattered, awakening within this state is most clear.
The filial son Lin Taiding requests a small-scale *can* (sermon) before the spirit to commemorate the first anniversary of the passing of his father, Layman Wenruo. The Master said:
"The ancients said: 'When the hundred members of the body have all decayed and scattered, one thing remains eternally enlightened. Now tell me, what is this thing?"

After a long silence, he said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time dare not look upon this with their true eyes; the patriarchs of successive generations have no choice but to remain tongue-tied.

Nevertheless, while the public office does not admit even a needle, private ways allow for chariots and horses. It is by means of this that the Buddhas of the three periods sit within a mote of dust and turn the Great Dharma Wheel;
it is by means of this that the patriarchs of successive generations awaken to the essence of the mind and transmit the Buddha’s life-force. (Text)

If you, Layman Wenruo, transcend the toils of worldly existence by this means and ascend loftily to the stage of Buddhahood, remember that from the beginning you have shared the same nostrils with all Buddhas and patriarchs;
throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, let not this be forgotten.
The layman Lin Yifu requested a small *can* (sermon) for the spirit of his deceased wife, Lady Chen. The Master said: "Sentient beings receive a body within that which has no body;
thus they undergo birth and death within that which has no birth or death. Were it not for the sudden opening of the true eye,"
The cycle of the six realms of rebirth continues without end. As for the "True Eye," how is it opened? Try to look:
before entering the womb, where was this birth-and-death? After the four elements have separated, where is it again?
Since there is neither before nor after, how could there be anything in between? To perceive something as existing is merely like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky.
Thus, the Elder Śākyamuni said: "If one knows these are flowers in the sky, then there is no cyclic existence, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death therein."
It does not exist because it is unconditioned; it does not exist because its fundamental nature is non-existent. To briefly explain the single phrase "awakening into the fundamental nature":

how can one say that fundamentally there are no marks of male or female, and how could there be names such as "sage" or "ordinary person"? Throughout kalpas it is neither born nor extinguished; in its manifestation, there is neither past nor present. Lady, you should simply understand it in this way.
A Small Lecture on the Mid-Autumn Festival. The Master said: "In the autumn sky, a single moon shines upon how many people.

Human faces naturally grow old or young, yet the moonlight has no 'old' or 'new. This very moon, which is without 'old' or 'new,' was never dark during the waning phase, never bright during the new moon, never deficient during the crescent, and never full during the full moon.
Worldly people look only toward brightness, darkness, and fullness."
Looking at the moon from a gap, one sees only the moon’s reflection; the true moon has not yet been seen. What, then, is the true moon?
After a long silence, he said: "When the eyes behind the head open, the true light illuminates heaven and earth."
The filial daughter Cao Xingtan and Cao Xingjie, along with the filial grandson Cao Hongzhi, have offered this memorial for their mother, Lady Xie, requesting a small discourse before her spirit.
The Master said: "Birth and death are not existence; Nirvana is surely not emptiness. If you wish to know the ultimate meaning, at midnight the sun is red.
Since Lady Xie passed away, five weeks have now elapsed. Tell me, what of this spirit?
Regarding the true nature: can the two characters "birth-and-death" be changed?

If they could be changed, then what is this "brightly shining, spiritually alert" thing that takes charge wherever it is? If they cannot be changed, how can one bear with this skin-bag being tossed here and there?
If you see this clearly, then whether they are changeable or unchangeable are both merely superfluous words. Why?
Indeed, this single period of birth and death is entirely like a dream from yesterday; it is utterly unattainable.
This very unattainability—when realized by the Buddhas—is called Great Nirvana; when deluded by sentient beings, it is termed the beginning of birth and death. Lady, you must turn toward this point.
The eye of wisdom is opened wide; one sees through to the very source. At such a moment as this, tell me: where is Lady Ju?
The autumn wind blows through the bamboo door; the bright moon shines upon the mountain gate.

The filial sons Zhang Shizhan and Zhang Shimei, who have succeeded to the lineage of the late Mr. Zhaotao, offer this memorial service for their father, Mr. Qingfang, and request a small *canshen* (private sermon) before his spirit.
The Master said: "This hundred-year body is fleeting and fragile; whether it remains or departs, do not grieve or rejoice.
This body is like foam upon the water—its gathering and dispersal have no fixed end. To realize that this body is empty is to realize the Vajra-body: neither born nor extinguished, without..."
It has no end and no beginning; all myriad virtues are perfectly complete. Difficult to compare within the three realms, in a single thought-moment one suddenly returns to the source.
Right where one is, one transcends birth and death. As for the very path of returning to the source—where does it lie? After a long silence, he said:
"Realize it before your parents were born. Be careful!"

For the General Governor of the Provincial Circuit, Lord Li, the Master presided over a small funeral sermon at the spirit altar. He said: "I respectfully venerate the General Governor of this province, Lord Li.
Six or seven years have passed since you departed this world. The clerks Zheng Xue and Ye Shiyin and others have attended by your side morning and evening;
your meals and your instructions were provided most exhaustively. Thinking there was no way to repay your profound kindness, I have specifically come forward..."

At Gushan, he performed repentance rites and provided meals for the monastic community to dedicate merit to the deceased. He further requested that I, a mountain monk, go to the spirit’s abode to preach the Dharma. Alas!

His virtuous influence endured among the people, and his meritorious achievements were recorded in the state annals. Yet, in a single day, he has laid down his burden; both the court and the commonalty lament his passing.

Nevertheless, within the three realms, there is no embodied being subject to outflows who does not die. Why is this? It is because they are constrained by form and confined by the limits of numerical existence.
Even so, one must know that there exists that which does not die. What is it that does not die? Is it the name that is immortal? Or is it the achievement that is immortal?
A name may eventually be erased, and an achievement may eventually be exhausted; there is only the capacity to establish achievements and create names [that endures].
It is neither born nor extinguished; it neither departs nor arrives. It is the pivot of the myriad transformations and the fundamental source of all living beings.
Though it manifests birth, it cannot be defiled by birth; though it manifests death, it cannot be altered by death. It appears in form, yet form cannot confine it;
it participates in the phenomenal order, yet that order cannot enclose it. It is vast and pure, transcendent and unimpeded.
Sentient beings are deluded by this, and thus birth and death are endless. The Buddhas awaken to this, and thus they are liberated right where they stand.
Yet, in delusion there is nothing lost, and in awakening there is nothing gained; there is only the difference between concealment and manifestation. Therefore, the Patriarch said:
Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; light and darkness are never separate. Now I entrust this dharma of concealment and manifestation—it is neither one nor two.
Do you understand this dharma, Master? A single ray of divine light illuminates heaven and earth; the myriad phenomena are viewed within a mirror.
I humbly entreat you to take care of yourself.
To Fang Shengmu, Chief Censor: I respectfully present this memorial for the late Great Honored Father, the Elder Layman Guangyan, and request a small discourse before his spirit.
The Master said: "The late Elder Layman Guang was wealthy yet frugal; noble yet increasingly humble; and as he grew old, he became only more vigorous."
That he was compassionate yet stern is something known to all people of this world.

However, that he clearly discerned sin and merit, extensively practiced manifold virtues, cultivated the purity of *dhyāna* with the aspiration to ascend to the nine lotus realms, and was diligent in ritual worship and recitation—such that his merit and wisdom became profound and firm—is not something known to the common people.
Since our late father passed away, seven weeks have already elapsed; thus, he has not yet been reborn.
The blessings and rewards of the human and celestial realms are fully possessed life after life;
how much more so for the Great Ancestor, whose aspiration does not lie in the human or celestial realms, but in the Pure Land? Nevertheless, Daopei has something further to add.
In the past, when Chan Master Panshan Baoji was going out one day, he saw a funeral procession being carried along. The funeral singer shook his bell and sang: "The red wheel is certain to sink..."
He went west. It was not yet known to which direction his soul had gone. From beneath the curtain, the filial son wailed, "Alas! Alas!
Hearing this, Panshan’s body and mind leaped with joy, and he attained great enlightenment. But tell me, what did he realize? "Alas! Alas!
His father had, right here and now, directly grasped that which has been the matter throughout kalpas of time; it is present in this very moment, manifest and perfectly luminous. It is finished.
There is no deficiency or surplus. As for this coming and going of birth and death, these Sahā worlds and Pure Lands—what are they but heat-haze and flowers in the sky?
Do you understand, dear father? The nostrils are right upon the lips; there is no need for weary toil to seek them elsewhere. I pray you, take care.
Ma Faxiu, on behalf of Duke Wang Gong, requested that the Master preside over a small *canshan* (private sermon) before the spirit tablet. The Master said:
"The filial son Wang Mei, and the filial grandsons Xi Sheng, Xi Xian, and Xi Yin, for the sake of the late Duke Wang Gong, whose courtesy name was Jiben, and the late Lady Li:
since their passing more than forty years ago, you have constantly cherished the kindness of their nurturing and the virtue of Heaven’s bounty."
In response to your report: My grief is profound within my heart. Now that I have been honored by the bestowal of your imperial decree, a radiance has descended as a blessing upon this grave.
Therefore, I shall seek blessings from the Awakened King and return my sincerity to the ocean of the Sangha, performing great Buddhist rites to offer a small measure of filial devotion.
I further request that the mountain monk go to the presence of the spirit to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. May the spirit listen attentively:
All sentient beings within the three realms are without exception subject to the suffering of the cycle of birth and death. Thus the World-Honored One said, "This Sahā world is a land of hardship.
If one wishes to emerge from this difficult land of birth and death, one must directly uproot the very foundation of birth and death and reach the state of non-arising.
The place of death. This is the place where there is neither birth nor death; it is precisely where a person establishes their body and sustains their life.
As for the very root of birth and death, how can it be uprooted? *Tut!* What do you call "birth and death"? Birth is like floating clouds arising in the vast void;
death is like bubbles dispersing upon the great ocean. To perceive the marks of birth and death as being real is itself—
It is like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky. As for that place where there is neither birth nor death—how can one ultimately reach it?
[The Master] holds up his whisk and says: "Do you understand? When a Son of the Buddha dwells in this stage, he is the very enjoyment of the Buddha;
he is constantly within it, whether walking, pacing, sitting, or lying down. Great Lord and Great Lady, simply cast open the true eye right here and transcend directly.
Depart. Farewell.
Master Xi-qing was invited by Li Gongjian’s parents to offer a small *can* (sermon) before the spirit tablet. The Master said:
"The filial son Li Ying and Sun Xiying [offer this] for the sake of Lady Li Gong Yongping, and the late ladies Lady Dong, Lady Wang, Lady Su, and Lady Wen, who have passed away."

It has been a long time since [his passing], yet my sorrowful longing remains undiminished. I reflect that were it not for the grace of the Triple Gem, it would be difficult to repay his boundless virtue.

Therefore, I have come specifically to Mount Gu at this time to provide meals for the Sangha, perform repentance rites, and extensively carry out Buddhist services to assist his spirit. I have further requested the mountain monk to preach the Dharma to provide guidance.
Listen attentively, O Spirit: In the past, at the assembly on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: "The wondrous..."
The nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks. Originally, there have been no worlds and no sentient beings.
Because of delusion, there is birth; because of birth, there is extinction. To eliminate extinction is called "delusion"; to eliminate delusion is called "truth.

Thus one knows that the sentient beings of the three realms, due to being obscured by this perfectly luminous wondrous nature, establish names within the nameless and establish marks within the markless, even amidst the absence of sentient beings.
Seeing sentient beings, one perceives worlds within worldless realms, giving rise to views of arising and ceasing and falling into the sentiments of ordinary and sage.
Therefore it is said: "Ordinary people see all phenomena merely following after their appearances; failing to understand that phenomena are signless, they do not see the Buddha.
If one can use the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm to illuminate all appearances as being like empty space, one will directly behold [the Buddha].
The Buddha-nature is primordially and eternally abiding; it is free from names and free from forms, neither arising nor ceasing. There is no world and no sentient beings.
This may be called penetrating to the very source of all phenomena and reaching directly to the other shore. Do you understand? "Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata."
Only then can one be called Avalokiteśvara. Great Lord and Great Lady, simply proceed directly toward this very point and attain transcendental awakening.
Be careful. Small Assembly Lecture.
It is said: The former Master spoke thus: "The sons of Śākyamuni falsely divide Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya; when viewed closely, they are all but the light of the One Mind."

The Master said: "Do you all wish to recognize the light of the mind? In Chan, it is subtle and continuous throughout the three realms; in the Teachings (Dharma), it is vast and expansive amidst the dust of the world;
in the Vinaya, Xiao He did not recognize it. I, this mountain monk, have thus made these critical distinctions. Now tell me: are they divided or undivided? If you say they are divided..."
Where is the division? If you say there is no division, how can one account for the fact that the three names—Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya—remain distinct?
If someone can discern this, I grant them the possession of the eye. Nevertheless, suppose a man were to come forth and ask: "Before light has even arisen, what is the mind?
*Ei!* Better to cut out one's tongue than to violate the national taboo.
The filial son Zhao Jing and others offer this memorial for their father, Master Xiansheng, and request a small discourse before his spirit. The Master said:

"Today, having read the biography of Master Zhao Xiansheng, I know him to have been a distinguished young gentleman. In his youth, he was renowned for his literary talent; in his middle years, he was renowned for his virtue and righteousness.
His talent was sufficient to serve as a seasoning in the imperial cauldron, and his conduct was sufficient to bring honor to both sovereign and parent. As for his dispelling of difficulties and..."
His manifold acts of compassion and his distribution of alms to the poor were all merely the overflow of his public virtue. When he suddenly passed away, everyone sighed with deep sorrow.

His filial sons, Zhao Jing, Xi, and Zhe, mindful that they could find no way to repay their boundless debt of gratitude, entered Gushan to provide meals for the Sangha and perform rites of repentance to dedicate the merit to his posthumous peace.
They further requested this mountain monk to preach the Dharma before his spirit. Do you know, sir? It is the awakened nature.

Perfectly luminous: birth and death are but a single dream; though the dream-land has a thousand variations, the person remains unmoving. It is because sentient beings, since beginningless time, have not awakened from the eyes of their dreams, racing about within the mind-consciousness and entangled within the sense-faculties and their objects. All manner of grasping and rejecting is nothing but saṃsāra. Were it not for the Dharma King appearing in the world to demonstrate the method of returning to the source, there would be no way to achieve liberation. This is precisely as [the sutras state]: ...
