There has always been this and that; the Western Paradise is before one's very eyes. Where is it not perfectly pervasive? It is eternally present upon the precious lotus throne.
Whether walking, sitting, or sleeping—on the fourth night of the first month of the Dingwei year—I led the assembly to perform the Great Compassion Repentance for the sake of the Duke.

He prayed to Avalokiteśvara to assist the Master in his rebirth. When the repentance ceremony was finished, he went to observe him; the Master had suddenly ceased breathing and lay prostrate upon his meditation couch.
I asked, "At such a time as this, what is it like? The Master replied, "I am the entirety of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
I said, "This is precisely where one experiences its fruition. The Master smiled broadly, joined his palms in gratitude, and after a long while, rose of his own accord and sat cross-legged.
He sat down and passed away peacefully. His worldly age was seventy, and his monastic seniority was twelve years. His remains were kept in the stupa for three days.
After the cremation and collection of the bone relics, on the day of the Great Cold (Dahan) in the twelfth lunar month of that same year, they were enshrined in the Haihui Pagoda of the Śarīra Cave.
Daopai said: "When I was eighteen years old, I traveled to Dongyan and passed through Tanyang, where I met you at Miaogao Peak.
Seeing that you wore Confucian robes yet practiced the Buddha-way, our conversation was most joyful, and I knew you were a man of the Way.

Twenty-four years later, when you entered Gushan to receive the tonsure, I was able to share a hall with you; it was like meeting again after the passing of an entire lifetime, bringing me joy beyond measure."
Beyond my expectations, within two years, the former Master passed away. I, being unworthily his successor, appointed the Venerable Gong as the instructor for the newly ordained monks;
this was based on virtue rather than seniority. Though the Venerable Gong was nearly seventy years old, his vigor remained like that of his youth.
He constantly engaged me in mutual inquiry regarding these matters, and whenever he grasped the essence of a single word, he would never fail to dance with his hands and feet. Now, observing...
The final section of this light reveals that what has been attained is not shallow; therefore, I transmit it to demonstrate it to all who come.
Recorded.
Record of the Reconstruction of the Wansui Pagoda:
In the past, during the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty, the Prince Loyal and Magnanimous of Min established a temple on Mount Bu at the southeastern corner of Fucheng.
It was named Wansui (Ten Thousand Years) as a prayer for blessings. Behind the temple, he constructed a seven-story brick pagoda one hundred [chi] in height.

It was fifty *chi* high and visible from the entire city; it was exceedingly magnificent. From the Liang dynasty until the present, nearly a millennium has passed, during which time it has been renovated on numerous occasions, making its history difficult to verify.
During the Chongzhen era, the abbot Jing’an once solicited donations for a major reconstruction.
In the Jihai year of the Shunzhi reign, a great hurricane struck, causing the tiers of the structure to peel away. Furthermore, a large banyan tree had grown upon the upper tier of the hall.
Yimwei, the grandson of Jing’an, was able to uphold the legacy of his ancestors. He consulted with the local dignitaries, Lord Fang and Lord Ke, who generously donated gold to initiate the project.
Various officials and faithful devotees each joyfully offered their support.

Construction began on the *jiawu* day of the fifth month in the second year of the Kangxi era (the *guiyou* year), and it was completed on the *gengchen* day of the seventh month. The total expenditure amounted to two... [taels] of silver.
It weighs over a hundred *liang*. It is solid and dense both inside and out, sufficient to endure for a long time. When the work was completed, he humbly requested that I record these matters.
I have heard that wherever a stupa or temple stands, it is as if the True Body of the Tathāgata is present there;

the eight classes of devas and all the benevolent deities who protect stupas will guard it day and night, scattering flowers as offerings. Furthermore, a stupa is so named because it rises high enough to pierce the clouds and reach the Milky Way.

To manifest its extraordinary excellence, so that all sentient beings with teeth and hair may see it as soon as they lift their eyes; and by a single gaze or a single prostration, plant the seed of Bodhi.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "If a person, even with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple and once utters 'Namo Buddha,' they shall all together attain the Way of the Buddha.
Thus, the construction and repair of stupas are intended to provide for the multitude of living beings throughout the great earth.
This establishes the causal conditions for attaining Buddhahood; furthermore, it constitutes an offering to the true body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata.
Its merit and benefits are inconceivable. How could this be merely a trivial matter for the sake of saving labor or creating a grand spectacle?
It must not fail to be recorded; therefore, I entrust it to the scribe.
Record of the Reconstruction of the Mahā-vīra Jewel Hall at Kuangxiao Temple Fusha occupies the upper reaches of the Eight Min regions.
Its mountains and rivers are pure and auspicious; its climate and scenery are tranquil and beautiful. Moreover, the local customs are exceptionally inclined toward the Buddha-vehicle.

Throughout the four suburbs of the prefectural city, Buddhist temples are spread out like chess pieces, their bells and chimes echoing one another—a scene that rivals Mount Song and Mount Shao in Luoyang.

Regarding West Lake in Hangzhou: Guangxiao Temple is located south of the prefectural seat, about two li from the city walls. It is separated from the dust and clamor of the shore by a rainbow bridge that spans the water.
With Mount Shizi at its back and the twin waters facing it, its scenic beauty is unsurpassed; moreover, the temple grounds are vast and expansive.
Winding paths lead to layered gates, with long corridors and vast halls. The golden countenances of the Buddhas shimmer brilliantly, and the *śāla* groves flourish luxuriantly.

To those who approach with faith to pay their respects, it seems as though the palaces of Brahmā, Śakra, or the nāgas have descended from the void; they are unaware that they themselves remain in the human world.
According to ancient records, the temple was founded during the Six Dynasties; it received the imperial plaque "Lungxing" in the Tang dynasty and was known as "Jingde Tianning" in the Song.
During the Wanshou era, it reached the Shaoxing period, when its current name was bestowed. At the end of the Yuan dynasty, the temple fell into disrepair due to the ravages of war.

In the second year of the Hongwu reign, the monk Yuansong, along with his disciples Huikai and Wenjia, reconstructed it together. This was supported by the Grand Preceptor, the Honorable Yang Rong, titled Wenmin.

There were stele records for each of these, including that of the Metropolitan Graduate (Zhuangyuan) Mr. Ding Gongxian; however, they were again destroyed during the upheaval caused by the island pirates in the *xinyou* year of the Jiajing era.
That same winter, the monk Yizheng and others first constructed a small hall of five bays. In the *bingzi* year of the Wanli era, Provincial Surveillance Commissioner (Zhongcheng) Mr.
Pang Shangpeng wished to remit the temple’s tax burden, and District Magistrate (Ouling) Mr. Zeng Shiyuan vigorously supported him, whereby [the goal] was finally achieved.
Using the funds from these donations and through further fundraising, he rebuilt the main hall, making it exceedingly magnificent. Ninety years have passed since then;

moreover, having undergone dynastic upheavals and been trampled by the hooves of warhorses, although the Buddha images remain as if alive, the tiles are shattered and the rafters are rotted, leaving the structure precariously prone to collapse.
In the *Ren-yin* year of the Kangxi era, Zhou Xiacheng, the Magistrate of Jian’an County from Shanyin, [took up the task].
In my leisure time from official duties, I went to visit this place. My seeds of wisdom were suddenly awakened, as if by a long-standing affinity.

I lamented how quickly the present differs from the past and how the rise and fall of things is never constant; I remained sorrowful for a long while. Thereupon, I specially donated my stipend to serve as an example.
He commissioned the temple monks Wuguan, Hongwei, and others to solicit donations for the restoration.
At once, the local gentry and commoners responded to his call, each contributing their resources to support the undertaking.

This project began its construction in the sixth month of the summer of the Renyin year and was completed in the tenth month of the winter of the following year, the Guiyou year, at a total cost of over one thousand taels of silver. It is magnificent.
It is truly firm and solid, as if fashioned like a bronze cauldron. Furthermore, in the late autumn of the following year, Jia-chen, I came from Shigou to Baoshan.
There, I was requested by Guan Hongwei and others to compose a record. Observing that their meritorious deeds had reached completion, I did not decline and spoke these words:
"In the past, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One entrusted the Buddha-dharma to the kingdom."
Regarding the King’s ministers: they consider that in this degenerate age of the *mofa*, the true Dharma is fading and its essence is becoming thin.

Unless there is a powerful *mahāsattva*, it will be impossible to revitalize it. We respectfully observe that His Majesty, ascending the precious throne at a tender age, governs both within and without the realm;
he has everywhere promoted and honored the Triple Gem and extensively propagated the spirit of the school. Furthermore, Lord Zhou, as a distinguished scholar-official (*mingjinshi*)...

Rising from his post, he was appointed to govern a great prefecture. In the intervals between his administrative duties, he was able to apply himself with refined devotion to matters beyond the mundane world.

He renovated ancient temples that were on the verge of collapse. Thus, the sagacious sovereign and worthy ministers joined in manifesting this endeavor, leading the people toward perfect enlightenment and contributing to the eternal prosperity of the imperial domain.

To investigate the ultimate reality of these achievements, one finds they all originate from the assemblies of the Buddha; they do not forget the Buddha’s entrustment and accord with the vast [Dharma].
This is simply due to the power of his great vows. Formerly, the father of the Tang Prime Minister Pei Xiu was Pei Su.

In a previous life, he had been Xu Xuandu, who built a pagoda in Yuezhou; he passed away before its completion and was subsequently reborn as Xiao Cha, the grandson of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.
He went to visit Chan Master Tanyan to have him enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and observe his past causes and conditions.

The Master said: "Xu Xuandu, why have you come so late? The stupa of yesteryear remains as it was today. Later, the assembly requested the Master to repair the main hall of Longxing Temple. The Master said, "This is not for me to do.
Three hundred years hence, there will naturally be a lay patron (*puṇya-kṣetra*) who is not clad in monastic robes. He then inscribed this upon it. This reached the Tang dynasty... [and so on].

He was born as Pei Su. Indeed, it was just as he had said. Observing this, we see that formerly, when Master Zeng, the Magistrate of Ou, donated temple taxes, Master Pang, the Governor, constructed this hall.
Less than a hundred years later, the hall had already fallen into decay.

Yet, just as Zhou Gong arrived at the newly established prefecture, he personally initiated the fundraising for its repair, restoring it to its former splendor. How could one know that Zhou Gong was not [the very person foretold]?
In the past, Lord Liṅgong, by virtue of his vow-power, has returned once more. Cause and effect do not fail; this matter is not in vain.
Thus, he has specially manifested it to inform those who come after. This serves as a record.
*Record of Master Zhibai Xuan’s Rebirth in the Pure Land at Ziyun Foding Hermitage*.
I have heard it said by the ancients: "In the Buddha-dharma, what matters is this: if you can practice it, that is enough.

This is because one enters the Buddha-dharma and leaves the household life fundamentally for the purpose of transcending birth and death (*saṃsāra*). If one cannot practice, then one will gain no power over birth and death. How [could one otherwise succeed]?
This is what may be said regarding the Buddha-dharma. Observing those who have left the household life in recent times, I find those who can truly be called practitioners to be exceedingly rare.
Consequently, upon reading the biography of the Venerable Xuanzhi (Zhībái Xuán), I was moved by it alone. The Master was a native of Wēnlíng;

his surname was Zhèng, and he was the second son of the Gentleman of the Court for Consultation, Qīnchū. In his youth, he studied Confucianism. He married a woman of the Chén clan and fathered a son, who was the Venerable Xuánwén.

As for Master Wen, he was untainted by worldly affairs from his youth and aspired to transcend the mundane. When Lady Chen passed away during his middle years, he and Master Wen adopted a vegetarian diet and cultivated the Pure Land practice.
Upon Master Wen’s ordination, they lived together in a hermitage at Ziyun, where the Master attended to him while his own resolve for pure cultivation grew ever more steadfast.
He remained unconcerned with the myriad affairs of daily life, sitting in meditation within his single room, never ceasing to recite the Buddha’s name until he reached the age of eighty.

Tenth: When I arrived at Kai-fa Temple, he immediately followed me in shaving his head, donning the dyed robes, and receiving the precepts. He sighed, saying, "Who would have expected that in my declining years I would encounter such a sublime opportunity?
His joy was beyond measure. After two years had passed, one day he manifested slight illness; reclining upon his meditation couch, his breath grew faint.
He then entrusted a message to his lay patrons, saying, "I shall see you there in the Western Land. He further engaged in a dialogue with Ziwen.

Having finished [his recitation], he rose and sat in the full lotus posture. He passed away while recollecting the Buddha at the hour of the rat on the seventh day of the ninth month in the Jiachen year of the Kangxi era.

Alas! I have been a monk since childhood until my hair has turned white, yet I have treated the single phrase "Namo Amitābha" like a child learning to speak—reciting it and immediately forgetting it, never attaining mastery. You, however, shaved your head at eighty; in only three years, you have achieved this.
At the time of his death, his right mindfulness was clear and distinct; his spirit remained undisturbed as he sat in meditation reciting the Buddha’s name and passed away.

There is no doubt that he was reborn in the Western Pure Land. This was surely the result of his having clearly realized, deeply believed in, and effectively practiced [the Dharma] throughout his daily life.
Within the Buddhist Sangha, if there is one such as Master Gong, then even the single word "practice" can be considered free from reproach. Formerly, Pārśva...
The Venerable One left home at eighty and realized the fruit of Arhatship in three years; the Duke was tonsured at eighty and was born in the Pure Land in three years.

Although there is a difference between the present and the past in terms of time, the principle is in fact the same; therefore, I have specially recorded this to serve as an example for those who come after.
This is the record.

This flower and porcelain vase within the stupa inscription of the Venerable Elder Qinglin contain the sacred remains of the Venerable Elder Qinglin. The Venerable’s name was Rujian; he was from Hougan.

The son of the Lin family resolved at the age of eighteen to aspire to the Way. He crossed the mountain ridges to pay homage to Yunqi, and subsequently studied under Master Zhan of Xiansheng, whereupon he attained realization while contemplating the "Mu" (No-character) kōan.
Later, he returned to Fujian to visit his parents; upon his tonsure, he once again crossed the ridges to attend upon Master Zhan.
After a long time, he returned to Mount Gu and resided at Dong’an.

When Master Wuyi of Boshan began to propagate the Dharma on this mountain, [Yuanxian] devoted himself to him with sincere heart from his youth and eventually attained the essential meaning of the teachings. From then on, he deeply concealed his talents and practiced in secret refinement.
At the age of eighty-seven, he manifested his passing at his former hermitage in Shilin. Upon cremation, the flames were golden in color and the fragrance was rich and pervasive.

The wooden rosary he habitually carried did not break. On the day of the Great Cold (Dahan) in the twelfth lunar month of the Bingwu year of the Kangxi era, Dao-pai, together with the Minister Lin Kongshuo and other lay devotees, requested that his remains be returned to the stupa of the Venerable Patriarch at this mountain.
This was respectfully recorded by the mountain abbot Dao-pai.
The Record of Mount Dazhao:
Formerly, the World-Honored One admonished the bhikṣus, saying, "You must not take pleasure in wandering through villages;

you should dwell in seclusion in mountain valleys and beneath forest trees, contemplating the teachings you have received in order to extinguish the root of suffering. Therefore, all who left the household life during the Buddha’s era...

There is none who attains the Way or realizes the fruits of enlightenment in vain. Yet, in this present age of the final five hundred years, when strife is firmly entrenched, those who have dyed their robes and shaved their hair are submerged in the toil of worldly defilements;
they ultimately do not understand for what purpose they have left the household life.

They frequently interfere in secular affairs and constantly violate the sutras and the vinaya, becoming objects of derision and disdain for laypeople and householders. If one seeks that which is correct...

Because he left the household life to cultivate the dharma of seclusion and remained unstained by the world, he was like the moon selected from among the stars—not that it was entirely absent [from the sky], but rather that it was rare.
Master Mingpuzhao was the son of the Zheng family of Longjiang in Yong’an.

Having studied Confucianism in his youth, he attained a profound realization of the transience and illusion of worldly existence in middle age and resolved to seek transcendence. He then abandoned his home and entered the service of the West Hall Master Li Fan at Boshan, where he shaved his head.
Having received the precepts, he then contemplated seeking out an *āraṇya* as a place for authentic practice. He eventually found Mount Lan at Qingxi Forest;
there the woods were lush and verdant, and the springs and bamboos were pure and clear. Seated amidst gongs and cymbals, he faced the Golden Turtle.

The location was truly magnificent. He subsequently donated his robes and alms bowl to purchase the site and constructed several bays of buildings upon it, inscribing the plaque above with the name "Dazhao.

This was during the summer of the *jiwei* year of the Chongzhen era. By the *dingyou* year of the Shunzhi era, disciples had gathered like clouds, yet the hermitage was too narrow to accommodate them.
He therefore solicited contributions from the public to assemble the labor and materials for the grand reconstruction of a main hall, a central corridor, and two wings. Furthermore, on the left...
He constructed a five-bay pavilion; the right wing served as a hall for vegetarian offerings and a kitchen.

He further established farmland to provide for the needs of incense and lamps, and built a stupa as a place for enshrining relics. Thus, the Dazhao Daochang became resplendent, emerging as a preeminent monastery in the region.
Today, Master Zhao is over seventy years of age, yet his spirit remains vigorous as he cultivates the Pure Land practices and recites the Lotus Sutra daily.
There was no leisure moment; yet all his disciples were able to deeply embody their master’s intent and diligently refine their practice.

Standing tall beyond the mundane world, they remained untainted by worldly defilements. Are these not truly bhikṣus of the Dharma-ending age who have been able to look up to and follow the Tathāgata’s clear instructions?
The eminent monk Wuya, a preeminent disciple, has truly overseen this undertaking from beginning to end and has specifically requested a text from me to be engraved upon stone.
To ensure its endurance for all time and to illuminate the practice of the public way, I— who have long held him in deep respect and admiration— have not declined to set down these words,
despite their lack of refinement,
and have thus composed this record of the reconstruction of the Haoguang Pavilion and the Canxiang Hall.

Now, the Sangha is counted among the Three Jewels and serves as the great field of merit for humans and devas. Dwelling together under the four seas, they should live in harmony and without contention;
practicing the Dharma together and eating from the same hall, they aspire toward the Way of Great Unity.

No object, whether large or small, once dedicated to the *caitya*, belongs to the ten directions. Should anyone treat such things as private property, they shall incur immeasurable sin before the thousand Buddhas.
Regarding those who have transcended the world, repentance is not permitted; this is the solemn teaching from the Buddha’s own mouth, as recorded in detail in the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Since the founding of this monastic community by National Teacher Shenyan during the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty, the lineage of Chan patriarchs has been passed down for over eighty generations.

Reaching the Dingmao year of the Tianqi era, the Venerable Master Wuyi of Boshan began the propagation of the Dharma at this mountain. With dragon-like and elephant-like disciples gathering like clouds, he established [the hall] within the Great Hall.

To the east, five bays of a hall were constructed facing west as a place for receiving offerings. Reaching the year of the Jiaxu cycle during the Chongzhen reign, our late master, the Venerable Yongjue, came to preside over this mountain.
He rebuilt the temple buildings and subsequently changed the orientation of the hall to face south.

It measured fifteen chi and three cun in length and sixteen chi and six cun in width, divided into two sections: the front served as the refectory, and the rear as the storehouse and quarters. Our late master...
After [the Master] had passed away, Dao-pai, being unworthy to inherit his legacy, succeeded him in guarding the mountain gate.
As the assembly of monks grew daily, the hall became too narrow to accommodate them. There was a great donor, Mr. Yang, whose secular name was Shijie and whose dharma name was Taolong;
he was a native of Gaizhou Prefecture in Guandong and a relative by marriage to Prince Jingnan, General Geng. Having entered Fujian with the imperial entourage, he retired from office for many years.

In his leisure time, he would frequently mount his horse to climb the mountain, devoting his heart to seeking the Way. Once, his seeds of wisdom suddenly blossomed; filled with profound resolve, he vowed to donate his wealth to demolish the old buildings.
He ordered craftsmen to select timber and constructed a great hall of five bays upon that very site. The upper level served as a storehouse and quarters;
all offerings from lay devotees and all necessities for the Sangha were stored within it. He named it "Hao Guang" (Radiant Light), taking [the name from]...
A portion of the merit from the Tathāgata’s *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair) serves the purpose of providing shelter for descendants;

below, it extends to form a refectory capable of accommodating five hundred monks seated in rows for their meals. It is named "Consuming Fragrance" (*Cānxiāng*), taking its meaning from Vimalakīrti’s invitation to the Great Assembly to partake of the fragrant food at the Gandhottamakūṭa.
Construction began on the twentieth day of the second month of the sixth year of the Kāngxī era, the *dingwei* year.
On one day, it was completed on the twenty-eighth day of the intercalary fourth month of this year. A total of over six hundred taels of silver was spent;
without seeking outside assistance, the lay devotee alone bore the entire burden, which may truly be called a feat of rare capability.

The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the south regard wealth as their very life; even when their treasuries contain worn-out strings of coins and their granaries hold aged red rice, they are unwilling—

To give lightly to others is rare; yet now you, Layman, have joyfully dispensed gold to complete this pavilion, storing the property of the *caitya* to provide offerings for the monks of the ten directions.
Had it not been for your having planted roots of goodness in the past within the truly pure field of merit of the Triple Gem, such a deed would not have been possible.
A profound and correct faith has been born within me. Who could achieve such a thing? Furthermore, the Sangha is that from which the Buddhas and Patriarchs emerge;

to make offerings to the Sangha is to make offerings to the Buddha. How inconceivable is the merit thereby obtained! Therefore, I have recorded this, engraved upon a slab of fine stone to endure for all eternity.
Preface to the Four Houses’ Verses on Ancient Cases.
Originally, ancient *gong'an* did not have verses. Verses began with Fenyang; after Fenyang, Xuedou followed in his footsteps, and their works are renowned as "Verses" (*song*).

The sages of antiquity have passed down this tradition, and each of the various schools has its own verses (*song*). Among those of the Dongshan (Caodong) school, three are most renowned for their verses:
Touzi Qing, Danxia Chun, and Tiantong Jue. Regarding these verses, there was originally no critical commentary;
such commentary began with Yuanwu. Following Yuanwu, Wansong and Linquan followed in his footsteps. Yuanwu commented on Xuedou, Wansong commented on Tiantong, and Linquan commented on Danxia.
Together with those of Touzi—these having been compiled by later generations—they were titled the *Sung-ku of the Four Houses*. Zen practitioners rely upon them as a guide.

I, however, maintain that the Way is fundamentally beyond words; no speech can reach it. The ancient venerable masters established models for the sake of sentient beings, bringing forth [the truth] in response to the immediate occasion like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint.
If one does not possess the discernment of the eye and the intimacy of the hand, it is already ten thousand miles away amidst the white clouds.
To attempt to praise it is like trying to trace the footprints of birds in the sky or count the tracks of fish at the bottom of a mountain stream;
one can only have a vague impression within the realm of imagination, let alone proceed to offer a critical evaluation.
Although these words were spoken out of compassion, they are like adding water to milk, which only serves to lose its original flavor. Those with true discernment will regret this.
Therefore, I have specifically omitted the commentaries and recorded only the original verses (*gāthās*) to be carved into woodblocks for publication, so as to share them with the world.
Should there be a monk of true substance who, upon seeing this, grants his heart’s approval, then the labor of my carving will not have been in vain.
If you think otherwise, the commentaries of the various masters are already available.

Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Foguo Yuanwu The Patriarch from the West came to point directly at the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha. Yet even at Caoxi, it was said:
"To speak of 'pointing directly' is already to have gone astray. How much more so for later generations, who entangle themselves in branches and vines, speaking of "investigation" and "practice"?
To employ various means of precaution and defense—is this not to bind people with substantial dharmas and thereby turn their backs on the clear instructions of our ancestors?
This is most certainly not the case. For the capacities and natures of sentient beings differ in ten thousand ways.

While it goes without saying that those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom may enter directly with a single stroke, as for those of middling or inferior capacity who have not yet been able to receive and bear the burden, they rely entirely upon the Supreme Person.
He emerged from his seclusion and spoke with bitter words out of compassion, skillfully applying expedient means.

Otherwise, how could he have rescued those of dry wisdom in the degenerate age and cured the chronic malady of fanatical learning? Master Yuanwu of the Song dynasty had studied extensively under various masters and experienced every kind of hardship.
Later, amidst the sensory phenomena of Yan’an’s Patriarch, he suddenly severed the life-faculty and succeeded to his Dharma.

Therefore, his recorded teachings for his disciples all emerged from genuine investigation and authentic realization, and from the diligent practice of pure cultivation. This was why he could strike away people's partialities and obscurations and spur them toward what they had not yet reached.
Daohui of Dongshan Gaofeng was a preeminent figure among the Chan masters; at the moment of his great awakening, he then became—
He said, "It is precisely the right time to practice Chan. He further remarked, "In all matters, simply remain humble, meticulous, and harmonious;

first prevent yourself from transgressing the three karmas, and maintain that one pivotal point directed upward, so that your brothers may progress toward it day by day. This was the case with Hǔqiū Lóng.
The Buddha’s wisdom and the people of the Flower Treasury World were all great figures of their respective eras.

Regarding the methods for self-cultivation and the essentials for engaging others within their teachings, there was nothing they did not treat with meticulous detail and thoroughness, never ceasing until every point was free from flaw or omission. As for scholars of the present day...
In terms of innate endowment and spirit, he was separated from those such as Dahuì by more than the distance between heaven and earth;
yet he discarded the merit of contemplative realization and moral practice, recklessly wishing to shoulder the heavy responsibility of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

How is this any different from a lame turtle chasing after a soaring dragon, or an ordinary person hoping for the rank of a Brahmā? The Master once said: "Among my fellow students, only Zhì [of] Longmén..."

I, Hai, have long since thoroughly investigated and clarified this matter. Yet, whenever I encounter conditions or meet with circumstances, it is never something I can simply set aside or overlook—not only for this life alone, but even to the end of the future, as one realizes immeasurable saintly bodies, this still would not be the place of ultimate rest.
Considering these words, those who truly understood this at that time were likely few indeed; how much more so, then, in the present age? How could one not find this strange?
Alas! I, Haisheng, was born late; moreover, I am as dull-witted and mediocre as any other.

Whenever I contemplate the flourishing of the Dharma-vehicle during the Tang and Song dynasties and the abundance of dragon-like and elephant-like masters, my heart does not fail to soar and my spirit to race, wishing to exert all my strength to reach such heights—but it cannot be attained.
Within this complete collection of the Master’s works, I have obtained these Dharma words; upon reading them, it was as if meeting with light in the darkness, or as if a poor man finding a treasure.

Although I, Pei, am not quick-witted, I shall put these words into practice. Therefore, I have transcribed them by hand and intend to carve them into printing blocks for separate circulation in the world.
A visitor raised an objection to me, saying: "This is merely the *Ji jia yu* (Family Sayings of Ji). You, Master, have mastered the Caves School (*Dongzong*).
Rather than taking that as your fundamental principle, you are instead so preoccupied with the words of another school; is this not perhaps a detour? I replied to him:

"The Buddha-dharma is the Buddha-dharma of one's own mind. Although various schools and gateways are established that appear to be different, when one reaches the ultimate and final limit, how could they..."
There are two points of convergence. Thus, a master once said: "The Buddha-dharma fundamentally has no 'self' or 'other. All schools are descendants of the Sixth Patriarch.

Upon careful observation of the meaning of the text, the preceding and following sections do not connect coherently; thus, the Zangben remains more reliable. Only then does one realize this.
This was not written by the Great Master’s own hand; rather, it may have been engraved by his disciples after his passing.

Now, having humbly collated three versions, we have striven to produce an excellent edition for publication and circulation. Let readers examine it carefully, and its merits and defects will become evident.

**Inscription on the Buddha’s Tooth** Some may doubt that this tooth is not indeed the Buddha’s tooth and mock me for erecting a stupa for it. I say: whether it is authentic or not cannot be verified.
However, I have observed that the Buddha’s teeth enshrined at Kaiyuan Temple in Jianzhou and Xiansheng Temple in Yuezhou are all similar to one another.
Therefore, it is enshrined in a stupa. Furthermore, among the ten bodies of the Buddha, there are the sentient-being body (*sattvakāya*) and the land-body (*kṣetrakāya*).
Thus, all that exists in the world—whether the environment (*āśraya*) or its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—is the Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya*. How much more so is this [tooth relic]?

It is just as when worldly people fashion images of the Buddha using gold, silver, copper, iron, earth, wood, or precious stones; one certainly cannot insist on [viewing them] as merely [material objects].

This is the Buddha; yet one must not cling to the notion that it is not the Buddha. How much more so for this towering jeweled stupa, which causes those who behold its form to give rise to faith, to resolve upon bodhicitta, and to awaken to and enter the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). What could be impossible about this?
Postscript to the Preface for the *Recorded Sayings of Master Shouchang* by Master Hanshan:
During the Wanli era, the Venerable Master Shouchang beat the "poisonous drum," and those who were struck by its poison and died were indeed numerous.
Yet, Boshan and Gushan arose in succession, becoming particularly prominent. Now, observing the Elder Master Hanshan...
On the *Shouchang Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Shouchang). It is said that Shouchang’s “pickaxe” is very much like the robe and bowl of the Yellow-Faced One;
these words do not fall short of the "entanglements" of Vulture Peak, yet they have been seen through to the very bottom.

As for the statement regarding "being poisoned by hearing sounds," those who experience such awakening and weep like Subhūti—how many people truly are there? It is those whose awakening is profound who are most deeply poisoned. Awakening.
There is no one whose tears flow with such intensity as this old man. How can it be said that there is no one in the world who understands his heart?
On a winter day in the year of Xinchou, while casually reading the *Complete Collection of the Old Man’s Dream Journeys*, I encountered this preface.
I have therefore recorded it at the beginning of the Master’s *Recorded Sayings*. Should anyone in the world or future generations see this record and be poisoned by its flow—
Tears are yet another thing brought forth by old age.
Regarding the calligraphy of Master Zinong (Hong Zi’er):
when I arrived in Wénlíng, I first met Master Zinong; I saw that his character was free from artifice and he moved with a carefree grace.
Beyond the dust and defilements of the world, though fame, profit, and official emolument were set before him in profusion, he ultimately could not be swayed from his resolve.

Furthermore, upon closely examining his calligraphic drafts for the "Nine Bends" poem of Ziyang, one sees that its lofty structure supports the heavens and its artistic ingenuity is uniquely realized;
in every dot and every stroke, he refuses to fall into the stylistic molds of the Jin and Song masters. Only then does one realize that this man was a figure rare to this world.
Yet this book is a rare work of its age; it should indeed be transmitted alongside this literary composition for ten thousand generations without decay. As the ancients said:
"In discussing a calligrapher’s script, one must consider their life as a whole. Even if Yan Lugu’s calligraphy were not technically refined, [it would still be esteemed for its character].
It should especially be considered a treasure rare in this world; how much more so since it is executed with such skill! Regarding this as well, I say to the Master:
these are the mountains and rivers from the brush of Master Cheng, inscribed for his dharma friend Xin Yu at the heart of the pond.
The hills and valleys within the breast of Old Xin and the landscape from the hand of Master Cheng—these two have suddenly met, and before one realizes it, they have merged.
All at once, it was revealed: ancient pines leaned over, and cliff rocks rose steeply. Wooden bridges spanned flowing streams that meandered freely;
thatched cottages and bamboo fences were as secluded and spacious as could be. Beneath the pavilion, sitting in conversation and dialogue with me was the Elder Xin;

we spoke together of non-arising (*anutpāda*). A guest approached, leaning on a staff and crossing the bridge; I did not know who he was, but observing his intent, it seemed he wished to seek [the Way].
The two of us discussed the matter at hand. He was truly a man of the Way. Beyond the distant peaks, there lies yet another celestial cavern;
it is something Master Cheng’s brush could not capture, and something Master Xin could not have conceived. I, too, became silent and forgot all words.
Huang Zijian’s Preface to the *Jie*:
The Buddha’s precepts are vast; yet, the precept against killing must be regarded as primary because its emotional impact is most grievous and its karmic retribution is most severe.

This is because the retribution for such acts is most grievous. The worldly people’s habit of eating meat is so deeply ingrained that they cannot abandon it all at once; therefore, he merely enjoins them to gradually refrain from it.

This is the intention of Master Huang to save the world. His prescription of the six monthly fasts, the ten monthly fasts, and the three annual long fasts is, moreover, a commentary on Confucius’s injunction against hunting when the nets are not in order, and Mencius’s principle of not seeing or hearing of certain things. Is this not indeed so?
When this work was completed, he requested a preface from me. This is something I have long delighted in discussing; thus, I have jotted it down at the beginning of these scrolls.
To inscribe upon the *Qingming Shanghe Tu*:
"The universe as a whole is but one great painting. Now, observing what Qiu Shifu has produced regarding the *Qingming Shanghe Tu*...

The *Hetu* (River Chart). This is a painting upon a painting; although it depicts the sublime topography of mountains and rivers, the crisscrossing streets and markets, the bustling throngs of carriages and horses, and the chaotic intermingling of people—all rendered with the utmost exquisite detail—nevertheless, it is but a single hair from the tail of a nine-headed ox.
Layman Yang Tianqu kept this scroll in his collection and commissioned me to write a colophon. Unable to refuse, I have added yet another layer upon the tip of that single hair.
This is merely a matter of brushstrokes. Let this fascicle rest for now. Just consider the universe: what great painting is it?
Ultimately, by whom was it created? Three dots are like flowing water; the curves resemble sickles used for reaping grain.

Inscription for the *Gobatsu-zu* (The Bowl-Stealing Figure) by Qian Shunju of the Yuan Dynasty, preserved in the collection of the Marquis Dong Wang. This *Gobatsu-zu* is of the utmost exquisite refinement.
The Sūtra states: "The Mother has ten thousand sons, all of whom are kings of ghosts; they are fierce, violent, and malevolent. Day by day...
They devoured the children of the people, who could no longer endure it and went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha took his young son Piṅgala and hid him beneath the base of his alms-bowl.
The mother then led her various ghost-children—namely, the spirits of plants and trees, the spirits of houses, the mountain spirits, and the stone spirits.
The birds, insects, spirits, and others all rushed forward, each exerting their supernatural powers to pull the celestial chariot and seek Piṅgala, yet they could not find him.

Their state of panic and their expressions of grief and longing were so vividly lifelike that one could not help but think of Hārītī, who daily kills and devours her own children without ever being satiated;
now that she had suddenly lost her own child, she would surely search for it everywhere.

He searched for him, crying out to heaven and weeping to the earth, going everywhere without exception. Upon seeing the World-Honored One, the Buddha merely instructed him to extend the love he felt for his own son toward the sons of others;
at that moment, his murderous intent was extinguished. He vowed to return to the precepts and realized the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Furthermore, he made a great vow to protect all sentient beings with merit, such that any person in the kingdom without a child might seek one from him.
To all such [beings], he gives them everything. Viewed in this light, the transformation from the mundane to the sacred occurs in but a single thought-moment;
what difficulty could there be? This scroll is not only a marvel of artistic execution, but its intent to admonish the world is profoundly deep.
That Master Xiu preserved it to bequeath to his descendants—could this have been without purpose? I respectfully record these words at the end of the scroll.
The Inscription for the Stone Pagoda Pavilion of Hegui:
The name "Hegui" (Combined Edges) was derived from a massive rock upon the mountain stream. Within this pavilion there once stood an Aśoka stūpa;
it is unknown in what year it was constructed. From its pinnacle down to its base, the stone is everywhere broken and chipped, with not a single part remaining solid or intact.
The supervisor Chengyuan then donated funds to rebuild it.

His intention was that those traveling along the Tongxiao Road might, upon reaching this spot, give rise to a single thought of pure faith, join their palms and bow their heads, and thus plant the seeds of Bodhi—not merely for the sake of adorning this pavilion for aesthetic appreciation.
Once the work was completed, he respectfully recorded its origins as follows. At the time of the Kangxi [reign], the fifth...
Written on the twelfth day of the tenth month of this year by [Name], Resident of the Mountain.

Preface to the Re-engraved Editions of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-parivarta on Perfect Enlightenment*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, and the *Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna*.
A Memorial for Soliciting Donations:

Regarding the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, there are as many verses and phrases as there are atoms in the universe. Of those that have been transmitted to China, there are but five thousand fascicles;

furthermore, these have remained largely hidden within the Dragon Repository (the Tripitaka). Among those who have left the household life, there are often individuals who, throughout their entire lives, [do not...]
If even those who merely hear the names [of these teachings] can attain such benefit, how much more so for those who grasp their essential meaning and thereby comprehend the Buddha’s mind?
It is for this reason that the Buddha-dharma declines day by day and the monastic community sinks lower and lower; there is indeed a cause for this.

Out of compassion for them, the Venerable Masters of antiquity extracted the very essence of the Mahāyāna from the Great Canon and circulated it throughout the world, so that every person may receive, uphold, and practice it according to the Dharma.
These include the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the three patriarchal sutras, and the *Awakening of Faith*.
The *Lotus Sūtra* perfectly reveals the true mark (*dharmatā*); the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* skillfully demonstrates the true mind; the *Vimalakīrti* extensively discourses on non-duality;

the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* points directly to the essence to meet the capacity of beings; and the *Laṅkāvatāra* clarifies the realm of self-realized noble wisdom—the very means by which Bodhidharma transmitted the seal of his mind.
The three sutras contain the Tathāgata’s most urgent instructions from beginning to end, as does the bitter-mouthed admonition of Master Guishan.

As for the *Awakening of Faith*, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa took one hundred Mahāyāna sutras as his foundation to demonstrate the meaning of the One Mind, the Two Gates, and the Three Greatnesses with extreme clarity and detail.
These various sections are both concise in expression and essential in principle; they are like holding up...

When the main rope is pulled, all the subsidiary cords are raised; when the collar is grasped, all the threads follow in order. If one can truly master this principle, then there will be no remaining meaning left unexplained within the entire Tripitaka.
This is why, since the Tang and Song dynasties, the imperial courts have used these various sutras as examination subjects for monks, granting ordination only to those who pass.
Is it not for this very reason? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* has already been re-carved at Mount Lengyan, and as for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*...

Regarding the various sutras, they were currently incomplete. Those practitioners of meditation who were intent on clarifying the scriptures often suffered from the difficulty of obtaining their original texts.

The Abbot Jiuda Jing was moved by this and vowed to solicit donations to carve printing blocks, so that their circulation might become even more widespread and the gift of the Dharma even more extensive.

The single thread of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' wisdom-life depends upon this to remain unbroken. We pray that all patrons will each relinquish their impermanent wealth to together accomplish this rare Dharma.
In the past, the World-Honored One sacrificed his entire body to seek half a verse; Sadāprarudita sold his heart and liver to seek the Prajñāpāramitā.
How much more so for these several sections of the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure of the Mahāyāna? One need only sacrifice that which is outside the self.
These are transient riches acquired through extensive acquisition; furthermore, you have widely printed and distributed them to open the eye of wisdom for all living beings.

How can the merit and benefit of such deeds be fathomed? Someone may say: "You, Master, do not circulate the recorded sayings of the various patriarchs, yet you laboriously reprint scriptures such as the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*.
Is it not that you have abandoned your primary vocation to stray onto a divergent path?"
I said: "Not so. You tell me: what is it that is spoken of in the Buddhist sutras and the ancestral records?
The man was speechless. I said: "A lion bites a person; a low hound chases a clod. I have appended this here as well to resolve the confusion of those who are deluded.
The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra Recited at Ruiji Temple:
Now, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra reveals the ocean of fruition of all Buddhas and the source-nature of all sentient beings.
It provides the model for the five stages of practice through which Bodhisattvas attain Buddhahood, and it fully contains all dharma-gates, vast and complete. Formerly, when the Tathāgata first...

When attaining perfect enlightenment, [the Buddha] did not depart from the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*). What was taught in accordance with the nature of reality across the seven locations and nine assemblies constitutes the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden teaching;
it cannot be compared to the various sūtras of the Three Vehicles. As stated in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata":
"This precious sūtra does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for those of the True Dharma King, the Tathāgata."

Sons of the Buddha, born into the family of the Tathāgata and planted with the marks of a Tathāgata, you who possess these roots of goodness—if there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate would soon perish and vanish. Why is this? Because none of those belonging to the two vehicles have heard this sutra.
How much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, analyze, and explain it! Only bodhisattvas are able to do so;
this unsurpassed and vast Dharma-gate can only be received and sustained by those who possess the authentic vessel of the Mahāyāna.

Anyone who today is able, within this sutra, to see it, hear it, or rejoice in it, giving rise to even a single thought of pure faith—such a person is like the Devaputra Raśmiprabha, who upon hearing the Dharma proclaimed by the celestial drum, immediately transcended the ten stages.
If one does not give rise to faith, then though they see, they do not see; though they hear, they do not hear. They are like the śrāvakas sitting in the assembly, as if deaf or blind.
It is so. For the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, faith is that which enables entry; without faith, one cannot enter.
It would be like reaching a mountain of jewels and turning back empty-handed—one cannot help but miss it face-to-face.

The venerable monk Yin Rui, at the request of the many donors of Linpu, has completed the restoration of this ancient temple of auspicious traces. He now intends to solicit the faithful to chant and recite the Avatamsaka Sutra.
This great scripture establishes the seeds of the One Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden teaching; I have composed this preface on its essential principles to await those with a refined ear.
This is the fundraising appeal for Lingshan Monastery.
Lingshan is the source of our school’s stream. Now, while its descendants pervade the world, the pagoda lies neglected in the weeds and the temple buildings are shrouded [in ruin].
Regarding the Cold Clouds [Monastery], no one had inquired about it. There was Chan Master Youwu, the true successor of Tianjie.
Moved by a singular fervor in his heart, he specifically expanded its foundations, renovated the stone pagoda, and further established incense lamps for perpetual needs.

From over a thousand li away, I have heard of this and have pressed my palms together in joy. Having exhausted my meager strength to assist in these matters, I have again written these words to inform my fellow disciples.
I only pray that you all will lend your hands to jointly propagate the ancestral tradition; thus, our school would be most fortunate.
This Dharma gate is most fortunate.
A Memorial for Recruiting Donations to Bury Animal Carcasses:
We live in this final age, when the air is filled with the pervasive stench of slaughter. Among the masses of living beings, those who perish by untimely death are indeed numerous. For this reason...
Skulls in the desolate wilderness and coffins by the roadside, exposed for years, ownerless and without refuge—may benevolent men and gentlemen devise a plan to bury them;
this would be their primary duty. How can one know that these people may not be future Buddhas?
Could this not be the six kinsmen from a past life? This single act is of such vast and profound merit that it is truly inconceivable.

Lin Danzhang of Fucheng, a fellow practitioner whose roots of wholesome thought are deep and whose field of merit flourishes daily, has fulfilled his wish for a bountiful harvest and further resolved to gather extensively.
He has specifically informed his colleagues to join him in supporting this sublime undertaking at the Śītavana cremation ground.

Within this very state, one is precisely poised to awaken to the principle of non-arising. Amidst the waves of the ocean of suffering, what prevents one from extending a hand to rescue those drowning?

Sentient beings and the self are fundamentally one body; the holy and the ordinary are but a single mind. If each person is willing to accept this responsibility, then throughout the heavens, benevolence and longevity will surely prevail.
A Memorial for Soliciting Donations to Repair Lingyuan Cave:

The sublime landscape of Lingyuan is a wondrous sight of the Fujian province. Sages and worthies of both ancient and modern times have successively cast their eyes upon it, entrusting their impressions to verse and song.
These were engraved upon metal and stone, and their traces remain clearly visible for examination. However, as the years have passed, material conditions have not remained stable;
the ancient pavilions and hermitages have already fallen into ruin, and the stone walls and stone steps appear even more desolate and dilapidated. Thus, those who come to visit these sites—
Who among us would not be moved by the sentiments of past and present, and harbor hopes for its restoration?

Furthermore, while it is indeed a mark of frugal virtue to cherish such "money" (adū) tucked away at one's bedside, how does gathering such sublime scenes beyond the secular world differ from tending to one’s own garden? I only pray that those with great power and influence will [act accordingly].

I hope you will deign to pay heed to this. Although even Yao and Shun were still apprehensive despite their vast benevolence in aiding the masses, the delighting in mountains and waters is likewise the natural capacity of the benevolent and the wise.
I do not decline to speak at length, for there will surely be those who can appreciate the sound.
A Memorial for the Joyful Celebration of the Completion of the Newly Crafted Incense Image of Great Compassion:

The Imperial Qing dynasty governs the realm, and the whole world has turned toward benevolence; yet alone the Mien Sea has not yet found peace, with the winds and cranes constantly sounding the alarm.
Golden halberds and iron horses—the imperial army endures hardship and toil. Blood seas and mountains of corpses—living beings are submerged in suffering. Daopei and the virtuous person Chi Da...

For a long time, whenever my eyes met these sights, my heart was moved. Thus, I made a vow together with others to recruit a multitude to perform the *Mahākaruṇā-sādhana* (The Ritual of Great Compassion) for three years.

This was done out of a desire to move the vast, perfect, and unimpeded heart of great compassion of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, so as to repent for the karmic obstructions of the common people of this great earth and pray for peace and tranquility.
Since undertaking this task in the spring of the third year of the Ren-Kui-Jia cycle...
Soon, they saw the waves of the sea gradually subside, the mountain mists silently dissipate, the winds and rains follow their proper seasons, and the signs of a great peace appeared.

There was not a single person who did not rejoice and leap for joy. Consequently, they again solicited contributions from the masses to carve a precious image of a Bodhisattva out of *candana* sandalwood, which was enshrined in the Dharma Hall to serve as a perpetual object of merit and offering.
Once this was completed, there was further held a repentance ceremony to celebrate the occasion.
Regarding this undertaking, the expenses required are not small and must rely upon the collective contributions of many.
I earnestly hope that influential figures, high-ranking officials, and eminent elders will deign to lend their attention. For such a matter of great merit requires those of great merit;
thus, even a single incense stick, a single flower, a single gaze, or a single prostration—provided it flows from a heart of genuine faith—is none other than an offering to Avalokiteśvara.
With a heart of unimpeded great compassion, identical in essence and non-dual, you lead these people to the ground of awakening and assist the imperial destiny for eternal years.
Since merit has its source, this undertaking was not established in vain. I respectfully submit this memorial.
Petition for the Recruitment of Sculptors for the Great Buddha Image:
The image of the Honored One in the eastern hall of Mount Gushan was completed forty years ago, yet it has now been damaged by ants.
This may be because the faith of the donors at that time was not single-minded, and thus the merit they produced was likewise not firm. Nevertheless, the Dharma is such that...
Arising in isolation, it depends upon conditions to come into being. How could one know that the passing away of a preceding Buddha does not serve as the catalyst for a succeeding Buddha?
The Chief Administrator Chengyuan first conceived the intention to cast an iron Buddha to endure for all time; however, the scale of the project was vast and grand.
I did not dare to act rashly. Now, the consensus of the public opinion is that enlargement by molding is best. Let stone pillars serve as the skeleton and brick and earth form the body;
seal the interior with lacquered cloth and coat the exterior with gold. In this way, it can be ensured that there will forever be no infestation of ants.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "If for the sake of the Buddha, a person establishes various images, whether made of the seven treasures, brass, or..."

Whether made of red or white copper, white wax, lead, tin, iron, wood, or clay, or even fashioned by adorning them with lacquer and cloth—such people as these have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Thus we know that creating images of the Buddha serves as a causal condition for attaining Buddhahood;
it is not merely for the sake of receiving blessings and rewards as humans or devas. Since the Parinirvāṇa at the Twin Trees, [the Dharma] has relied solely upon...

The Image Teaching is established to enlighten the deluded masses. Whenever members of the fourfold assembly burn incense, scatter flowers, prostrate, and make offerings before the honored images—even unto the point of generating the mind of unsurpassed bodhi—they all rely upon this as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
How could the merit and benefit thereof be limited merely to a single person? This very mind creates the Buddha.

This mind is the Buddha. Is it the mind? Is it the Buddha? Fundamentally, they are not two separate things. I respectfully set forth this essential meaning to inform those with whom I share this karmic connection.
Regarding the Memorial for the Construction of a Hermitage at Nan Yuan:
In front of Baiyun Monastery lies Nan Yuan, extending for some ten mu. Encircled by winding walls, its fruit trees grow in abundance.
Yin leans against the foot of the drum-shaped peak and faces the Three Mountains; it is a path leading to the heavens, a distinct realm above.
The fellow-practitioner Zhang Zaihui made a vow to construct a small hermitage within this area to enshrine the Great Being Samantabhadra. For Samantabhadra is the eldest son of the Avataṃsaka;
his vows and practices are vast and expansive, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm throughout the limits of the future. There is no... [end of text]

This reaches the ultimate limit. In the aspirations of Laozi, there is something to be derived from this. Having already contributed his own funds to initiate the project, he further commissioned me to write these words to inform his fellow practitioners.
I respectfully record its origins here; surely there will be those who can appreciate its true resonance.
A Universal Exhortation to Practice Nianfo and Release Living Beings:
When a person is born into this world, how much of the hundred-year span of their life can truly be theirs? With a single breath not returning, it is as if one has been separated from them forever.
In this world, nothing of the myriad things can be taken with one; only one's karma follows the person.
At such a time, can one wish to utter even a single phrase of the Buddha’s name? Can one wish to spare even a single life? Therefore, I exhort all people of the world today:
regardless of whether you are noble or lowly, wealthy or poor, male or female, old or young, each and every one of you may turn back and apply yourself to the Way.

Seeing through this with one's own eyes, steal away even a single day of leisure to recite the Buddha’s name during the three periods of the day. By curbing extravagant and wasteful expenditures, one may save lives in peril and distress.
This serves as the primary cause for rebirth in the Pure Land and plants the seeds of compassion. What is called "reciting the Buddha’s name" does not mean reciting the name of some other Buddha;
rather, it means reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, for that Buddha has long held a solemn vow to gather [beings] into his embrace.

This is because one receives those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha so that they may be reborn in the Pure Land. As for "releasing life," it does not mean releasing other living beings;
rather, it means releasing one's own many lifetimes and one's six types of kinsmen and relatives.

This is because since beginningless kalpas, they have repeatedly been one's father, son, brother, or various other kin, differing only in that their forms have changed and their retributions shifted, such that they no longer recognize one another. How do we know this to be so?
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "From here, to the west, beyond a hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of Buddha-fields, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
In that land there is a Buddha, titled Amitābha, who currently dwells there, teaching the Dharma. It continues, stating:
"Upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, one should hold fast to his name for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days..."

Whether for five days, six days, or seven days, if one maintains a single-minded focus without distraction, then at the time of that person’s death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, will appear before them.
At the moment of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
The *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra* states: "There may be sentient beings who..."

If one can, with a sincere heart, maintain an uninterrupted voice and complete ten recitations, calling upon the name "Namo Amitābha Buddha," then by virtue of invoking the Buddha's name, within every thought-moment, one shall eliminate the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. At the time of the end of life, [one will...]
One sees golden lotus flowers, like the orb of the sun, appearing before that person. In the space of a single thought-moment, one immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one recollects the Buddha and contemplates the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha both in the present and in the future."
As stated in the three sutras above, is this not clear evidence that those who recite the name of Amitābha Buddha will be reborn in the Pure Land?
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "All sentient beings who possess life should constantly give rise to thoughts of benefit and compassion;
they should not even harbor ill will or afflict other beings, let alone conceive of others as mere sentient beings. Because...
One acts with the intent of committing slaughter. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that there are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat;

namely, that all sentient beings have, from time immemorial, been related to one another through successive causes and conditions as our own kin. Because they are regarded as kin, [meat should not be eaten].
One should not eat meat. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "Out of a heart of compassion, one should practice the act of releasing living beings.
One should form this thought: 'All men have been my fathers; all women have been my mothers. In every birth, there has been none from whom I have not received life.
Therefore, the sentient beings of the six realms are all my parents. To kill and eat them is to kill one's own parents."
My parents, as described in the three aforementioned sutras—could this not be clear proof that those who release living beings are releasing their own kinsmen from many lifetimes?
An ancient master said: "If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can be believed?
If one does not cultivate the human path, what path can be cultivated? Now, having been born into the human realm and having heard the words of the Buddha, yet one does not believe them...
As for those who practice [these teachings], I can do nothing for them; it is already too late.

Regarding the inferiority and excellence of this Sahā world and its Pure Land, as well as the causes and effects of the transgressions and blessings of killing and releasing life, these are all extensively recorded in the sūtras and need not be elaborated upon here.
I only hope that those of high intelligence will take the trouble to study them widely and convert those who have not yet believed; there is no greater merit than this.
A Universal Exhortation to Mindfulness of the Buddha:

It is the nature of all human beings to loathe suffering and delight in joy, to abandon suffering and seek out joy. Now, there exists extreme suffering yet we do not know how to weary of it or abandon it;
there exists supreme bliss yet we do not know how to rejoice in it or embrace it—is this not a profound delusion? As for that which is extreme suffering:
This Sahā World is characterized by birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as various forms of oppression.
As for "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī), it refers to the Pure Land of Amitābha Buddha in the western direction, where both the primary and secondary retributions are pure and magnificently adorned.
Because sentient beings have long been deluded and fail to comprehend the nature of suffering and bliss, the ancient masters combined these two lands and compared them, saying:
This [body] consists of flesh and blood; for all who are born, there is suffering. That [body], however, is born by transformation from a lotus flower; thus, there is no suffering of birth.
This [body] is subject to the passage of time, with decrepitude encroaching daily. That [body], however, is not shifted by cold or heat; thus, there is no suffering of aging.
This [body] is a body of outflows (*āsrava*), entangled by the suffering of illness; that [body], however, is a retribution-body (*vipākakāya*) that is pure and free from the suffering of illness.
This [life] is such that those reaching seventy are rare, for impermanence is swift; that [life], however, has immeasurable lifespan and is free from the suffering of death.

This refers to the affectionate attachment of kin; where there is attachment, there must inevitably be separation. That refers to the kinsmen of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); there is no suffering of being separated from those one loves.

This refers to enemies and adversaries; where there is enmity, there must inevitably be a meeting. That refers to the gathering of supreme goodness; there is no suffering of encountering those one hates.
This refers to the hardships of hunger and cold, with insatiable greed and seeking. That refers to clothing, food, and precious treasures.

As for this [present state], its enjoyment is manifest; it is a hideous physical form with many impaired and deformed sense faculties. That [state], however, possesses the marks and signs of excellence, and its body is endowed with radiance.
This [state] revolves through birth and death; that [state] has forever realized non-arising. This [state] makes the cultivation of the path difficult to accomplish;
that [state] directly ascends to the stage of non-retrogression. This [state] is filled with hills, mounds, pits, and ravines, with forests of thorns, earth, and stones.
Whereas these mountains are filled with filth and impurity, there the ground is of pure gold and jewel-trees reach toward the heavens;
where towers soar made of the seven treasures and flowers bloom in four colors, here the twin śāla trees have already perished and the Dragon-Flower [Buddha] has not yet appeared;

whereas there Amitābha Buddha currently dwells preaching the Dharma, and here Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta merely look up to their illustrious names; there he is together with those two superior beings.

In this [world], one's parents are the supreme friends; yet here, the various māras and non-Buddhists harass and disturb right practice, whereas there, the Buddha’s transformation unifies all, leaving no trace of māras or non-Buddhists.
In this [world], seductive forms and lascivious charms delude the practitioner, whereas there, the primary retribution is pure.
In reality, there are no women; these are merely malevolent beasts and *chimei* (goblins) clamoring together with perverse sounds.

There, however, waterfowl and forest trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma. When comparing the two lands, the conditions and environments are vastly different, yet the excellences of the Land of Bliss are infinite and cannot be fully enumerated.
Judging by this and observing it closely, the suffering of the Sahā world is already such as this.

The pleasures of the Western regions are likewise like that, yet the people of this world remain in a state of bewildered ignorance; they neither know how to rejoice in them nor feel weary of them, and they neither grasp them nor abandon them.

This is entirely due to the habitual tendencies of delusion accumulated over many lifetimes, which shroud their own minds so that wisdom does not arise and the discernment of principles remains unclear.
Alas! If a person lacks far-reaching foresight, they will inevitably face immediate distress. There is no one among the people of the world who does not know this.
To acknowledge that death exists, yet fail to establish oneself for the life after death in a favorable realm, is also a great error.

This is why the World-Honored One appeared in the world; through various skillful means, he exhorted people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, none of which was other than to point out to people the path to their destination.
As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says: "If there be good sons or good daughters..."
If one hears the name of Amitābha Buddha and holds it fast— whether for one day, two days, or even up to seven days—
with single-mindedness and without distraction, then at the time of that person’s death, Amitābha Buddha, together with a multitude of holy beings,
will appear before them. At the moment of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
In this land, if one recollects the Buddha with a single mind for even one day, two days, or up to seven days, one still attains rebirth there;
how much more so for those who recollect the Buddha with a single mind for one month, one year, or even until the end of their life—how could they fail to attain rebirth?

Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Infinite Life* states: "There may be sentient beings who have committed unwholesome deeds—the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts—and because of these evil karmas, they ought to fall into the evil realms.
If they can, with a sincere mind, maintain an uninterrupted sound and complete ten recitations..."

By reciting "Namo Amitābha Buddha," through the power of invoking the Buddha's name, one eliminates the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas in every moment of thought.
At the time of death, one will see a golden lotus flower, like a sun-disk, appearing before that person.
In a single moment of thought, one immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Now, even a person who has committed the ten evil deeds can, within ten moments of recitation, have their sins extinguished and attain rebirth by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows;

how much more so for a person of true faith who recites a hundred times, a thousand times, ten thousand times, or even unspeakably many times—how could such a person fail to have their sins extinguished and attain rebirth? Therefore, I...
I universally exhort all people in the world to steal moments of leisure amidst their busyness and recite the Buddha’s name every day—whether a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand times.

Upon completion, mark a circle; dedicate the merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land. Once the year is fulfilled, then calculate the total: how many tens of thousands of recitations have been performed in all.
I record this in this register. May I uphold it for as long as my life lasts, gradually accumulating pure karma.

May I now be illuminated by the light of the Buddha, so that my transgressions are extinguished and my merit increases, and may I ultimately be welcomed by the Three Sages to be surely reborn in the Pure Land. My practice shall be real, my vows shall be real, and my causes shall be true and genuine.
If one is willing to believe and follow [this teaching], such a person is a true dharma-companion.

Offerings. We respectfully present these at the memorial altar for the spirit of the Great Donor, His Excellency Li, Minister and Governor-General of this Province.

We speak thus: Alas! The Imperial Qing has encompassed the Middle Kingdom; yet Fujian is said to be difficult to govern, with its mountains high and seas obstructive. We are honored that you, sir, have held the mission of authority here.

His virtue and majesty were as thundering; when he issued his proclamations and commands, the mountains and seas were brought to peace. Amidst the bustling activity of both court and countryside, all sang the praises of his virtue:

it was as green as the azure sky, and as straight as a plumb line or a carpenter’s square. Last year, during the spring of the new year, I came to visit the Stone Drums; upon seeing them once again, they appeared as if I had seen them before.
I immediately poured out my innermost thoughts and advanced [his practice] with precepts and goodness. He then responded with a "yes," his face overflowing with joy, saying, "I wish to study this.

We parted for barely a year, yet he sent inquiries three times. I looked forward to entering the mountains again, hoping to board the vessel of wisdom; alas, I did not expect that one illness would cause us to bid farewell forever.
The myriad people of the world wailed as if they had lost their Heaven. As for me, I am a man outside the world who has long since severed all worldly sentiments.
With a heart of integrity and uprightness, I cannot help but shed tears. Though the physical form is illusory and transient, the spirit is fundamentally eternal and ever-new.

May you dwell forever among humans and devas, protecting the state and blessing the people. I venture to present this fragrant offering upon your sacred altar; I pray that you, O Honorable One, will not remain oblivious, but will deeply savor this intent.
Alas! May you partake of this offering.

This sacrifice was performed by Fangke Weng on the second day of the intercalary tenth month in the fifth year of the Kangxi era, the year of Bingwu, under the *jiazi* cycle, corresponding to the day of Jihai. [Offered at] Yongquan of Gushan.
The temple śramaṇa Daopai respectfully draws water from Longquan Spring and brews phoenix tea to offer a sacrifice at the spirit altar of the Great Lord, the Elder Layman Guangyan Fang.
He speaks thus: "Alas! Daopai and the Elder Layman have formed a worldly friendship for barely ten years.
The Layman has taken me as his Prajñā-boat, while I have taken the Layman as..."
The moat of the Dharma-city—whether in cold or warmth, motion or stillness, in glancing back or turning around—all issues from sincerity; it is not forced.
When Master Daopei was about to depart for Shigou, the Layman vowed to detain him even at the cost of his life. His words and tone were so resolute and vehement that he came to shed tears.
Master Daopei’s heart was moved, and he halted his journey there. Furthermore, for over ten years, [the Layman] has written with his own hand in profuse script.
[Your] inquiries have been constant, not failing for even a single month; the longer it has been, the more you have shown me respect, never showing the slightest slackening.
How is it that you, a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), act thus for the sake of the Dharma and for others? This autumn, you, sir, fell ill at an advanced age. Your son, Mr.

Shengmu, is traveling on official duty and has not yet returned, and your mother, who was living with you for support, has likewise not been by your side. My heart is filled with deep anxiety, and I do not know—
Upon his departure, he led the assembly of monks to pray to the Buddha and recite sutras, looking upward to invoke blessings for longevity.
He dispatched attendants to offer condolences three times, yet the layman ultimately sent the remains from the Gandha-kuṭi and his personal effects as a final parting gift. Alas!
How can one bear to speak of this? Nevertheless, the layman’s life in this world was complete and perfect, leaving nothing to be regretted. Why is this so? It is said:
Wealth, nobility, longevity, and progeny—may these be fully possessed in every respect. What cause for regret could there be?
Furthermore, he constructed the precious halls of Kaiyuan, cast the great bells of Lingyuan, carved the Pure Land of Longshu, and protected the monastic groves of various mountains.
Regarding all matters of the Dharma, whether great or small, there was none in which he did not exhaust his mind and strength; all of this was...
The tree remains imperishable within the Jetavana Grove, providing the resources for merit and wisdom throughout every lifetime.

As for his cultivation of kinship ties and his compassionate care for the orphaned and solitary, the higher his rank became, the more humble his virtue grew; the older he grew in years, the more vigorous his strength remained.
