Warm and kind, modest and gracious, he was truly a man of great merit and virtue among the elders of the City of Blessings. When he resided there...
Though ill, his spiritual mind was serene and not disturbed in the slightest degree. He gave instructions for his final affairs with complete clarity;

his right mindfulness was firm and concentrated as he sat awaiting the end of life. How is this different from Vimalakīrti, who emptied all his possessions and lay down on a single bed while suffering from illness?
When it came time for him to change his mat, Daopei sent a monk to bid him farewell with a verse:
He said: "When one's karma is shed from the Sahā world, the spirit returns to the Pure Land. Originally there is not a single thing;
it is like a bird escaping from its cage. The layman saw this and was delighted; he nodded his head in agreement and passed away shortly thereafter.

Thus, it is certain that the layman, by virtue of the power of his lifelong faith, the power of his merit, and the power of his vows and practice, will be reborn in the highest grade of the Pure Land. Observing this, we see that...
The worldly merit of the layman was already such as that, and his supramundane merit was likewise so.
When one speaks of perfection and completeness, leaving nothing to be desired—who could it be other than this layman? Why, then, should there be cause for grief?

One need only reflect that the Confucian school has lost its model and the Dharma gate has forfeited its external protection; amidst the clear wind and bright moon, [this loss shall endure] forever...
Bearing his path and righteousness in heart, he could not forget his feelings and would often shed tears.

For this reason, he has reverently offered tea and fruit as a memorial, composing this text to announce it clearly before the spirit-curtain. May the Layman behold it! Alas! May you still partake of this offering.
I composed these "Four Words of Warning" for my Dharma friend Wang Qigang. A native of Guanzhong, he was dignified, upright, and prudent, never vying with others.
Yet, I feared that as a monk he might become entangled in worldly affairs and fall into the four faults; therefore, I requested him to write these words as an exhortation. Thus, [they were written].
By taking up the words of both Confucianism and Buddhism to illuminate one another, this is not only intended as a remedy for Qigang;
it is also, in part, a means for my own self-cultivation.
Renru (Endurance).
A proverb says: "If one cannot endure small matters, one will bring disorder to great plans. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"Abiding on the ground of patience, being gentle, kind, and compliant, without being rash or violent, and with a mind that is not startled. Indeed, among all matters, both mundane and supramundane, none are accomplished without patience.
Yet one fails because of a lack of forbearance. If it is truly he who is right and I who am wrong, then the fault lies with me; how could I not exercise forbearance?
If it is truly he who is wrong and I who am right, then my heart is free from shame; what need is there for calculation?

Therefore, a student of the Way should realize that both things and self are fundamentally empty, and settle the mind like the earth, allowing it to be trampled at will by oxen, sheep, dogs, and horses.
To give rise to even a single thought of anger or resentment is called "patience.
To speak with a gentle air while being stern in appearance but weak within is the mark of a petty thief. The World-Honored One, however, employs harmonious words and speech of love.
When instructing sentient beings, one must always speak first with a smile. Harmony is the primal qi, from which heaven, earth, and the myriad things arise.
Should there be even a single instance of disharmony, the qi of discord and calamity will gather within one's own person.

One must not fail to exercise caution. Therefore, those who study the Way ought to level their minds and hearts and soothe their speech and countenances, so that when others behold them, their [malicious] intentions are dissolved.
This is called "harmonious energy" (heqi).
The *Book of Changes* says with caution: "That which gives rise to disorder has speech as its ladder. The Sūtra says: "Guard the mouth as one would a sealed jar.
This is because, among the three karmas of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the karma of speech is the most serious; the flourishing or ruin of a state depends upon a single word. One...
Once words have been uttered, even four horses cannot overtake them; therefore, one must not fail to be cautious.

Thus, when a practitioner of the Way has anything they wish to say, they should deliberate upon it in their mind and measure it against principle. Free from flattery and crookedness, and being straightforward and sincere without artifice, only then should they speak.
In this way, there will be nothing that does not accord with the proper path; this is called "caution in speech."

The *Yì* says, "Moderate one's food and drink. The *Śālistamba-sūtra* (The Bequeathed Teaching) says, "Moderate the body and eat at the proper times. This is because sentient beings of the desire realm subsist upon food;
if there is even a slight lack of moderation, a hundred ailments will arise, leading ultimately to the loss of life. Therefore, one must be diligent in this regard when studying the Way.
The gentleman who disciplines the body follows established rules: he eats when hungry and stops before becoming full. That one may ward off illness and prolong life depends precisely upon this;
this is what is called "moderate eating."

This verse reveals the single phrase prior to the birth of one's parents for the Chan practitioner Zishan; even hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and patriarchs would find it difficult to know. Today, I shall speak it directly to you.
It is shattered. A stone ox swallows a wooden sheep.
To the Zen practitioner Xisheng, I show this ready-made single phrase:
Amitābha Buddha. In daily life and ordinary conduct, one keeps the gates of the mouth sealed; yet one day, suddenly, one personally recites it.
He has departed; his hundreds of thousands of marks and signs illuminate heaven and earth.
Once, as a layman, you assisted in offering prayers for your deceased mother; I offer this verse for you:

"In human life, it is precious to know that there is a beyond, so as not to fail the one who gave us birth. A hundred generations pass in the snap of a finger; the three minds flow swiftly like a rushing river."
The jewel in the garment was originally radiant; the treasure in the house was fundamentally complete. Once one awakens to the principle of non-arising, one transcends all entanglements.
To show this to those who practice Zen to the ultimate:

the original purpose of leaving the household life is to deliver oneself from birth and death. How could one willingly become a monk merely for the sake of rice and gruel? One must investigate a single phrase of the *huatou*.

Chè! Those from all quarters who attend Zen assemblies have traveled far, carrying their staffs upon their shoulders. When the heels are firmly planted, the thieving mind is extinguished; when the treasure-store is overturned, the family legacy flourishes.
If one does not seek the path of life at this very moment, treading on the frost, one truly fears it will lead to the solid ice.
I show the monks:
this floating life has its end, yet worldly affairs never reach completion. Who among you can awaken with such vigor as to come here and study non-action?
Wearing the three robes, one can endure the cold; with a single bowl, one forgets hunger. Like a lotus flower blooming upon the water’s surface, it rises tall and pure from the mud.
I tell you, Layman Guo Zhanqing, the Western Land is not far from here;
it resides solely within a single thought of the person. If the thought is defiled by the five turbidities, one is born [therein];
if the thought is pure, the nine lotuses immediately appear. Tear asunder the net of attachment to this Sahā world, and reveal the ancient face of Amitābha. Only those of great wisdom can do so.
Only a man of great capacity can possess such a sharp sword.
Makhali Muni returned to Kapilavastu;
originally of the lineage of the Western True Brahmā, he came to the Eastern Land to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, traveled throughout China, and has now returned.
Go! You must believe that the diligent journey does not lie upon the road.
To the Chan practitioner Zhi-shan, who supervised the construction of the three pagodas:
enduring both cold and heat, he did not shrink from toil; hauling stones and carrying mud, his efforts grew ever loftier. Five hundred years ago, he once donned [the robe].
Power! To employ it costs not even a hair’s breadth of effort.

I respectfully take up the Dharma-burden of the late Master Kongyin of Boshan and shoulder the Teacher’s responsibility. How can one suddenly emerge from the entanglements? The bowl and robe have a successor; his name may be known.

I offer my thanks. The family tradition remains intact; Master Daochang is steadfast. The wooden man has trodden through the moon upon the clear pool; the stone woman has overturned the heavens beyond the kalpas.
Whenever I recall your venerable kindness, it is now all gone; gazing toward the sacred curtains, my tears flow like a stream.
The path of the Chan Hall supervisor Huaxiu was originally a great highway.
Over many years it has crumbled and become impassable; let everyone lend a hand to repair it, so that the world may from now on be level and smooth.
On the fortieth birthday of my fellow practitioner Shouhui:

Since first entering the red dust of the mundane world, your mind has been intent on seeking the ford. In contemplating the river, you have found no difference; in yearning for the Way, you have perfected your spirit.
His lifespan extends through kalpas; his youthful vigor is like that of early spring. Since his innate faculties were never deluded from the start, why need he envy the pine and bamboo?

He shows us that the body and mind within a dream should not be clung to, and that the world within a mirror should not be craved. Let the light of the eye illuminate and shatter the three thousand worlds.
The realms. There is yet another profound gate above them.
Following the rhyme of Layman Tao Jishen’s "Entering the Mountains to Listen to the Dharma":

"I know you are able to silently realize this Way; you have cleared away the thorns and brambles from the path of awakening. Wearing a simple headcloth and carrying a staff and sandals, he enters the mountains.
Come! The fire of Māra that scorched the void has long since been extinguished. In the human pursuit of the Way, what is prized is the sincerity of one’s resolve.
One must here extricate oneself from the root-dusts of the senses; by personally tasting a single drop of Caoxi’s water, the feverish afflictions of the human heart are instantly purified.
To the Venerable Guxue of Longshan and the Old Ox of Tiantong:
Having reached nearly eighty years of age, you have given birth to a solitary unicorn of peerless excellence. You have swallowed up the West River and stirred its waves;
the myriad peaks and valleys are all overflowing. For years now, I have been too weary to move my lips for preaching the Dharma; I have returned to lie upon Longshan, hidden away.
The Big Dipper—ants craving the scent vie to rush toward it. Yet it causes the myriad phenomena to roar like lions. In the past, I once ascended Mount Taibai;
my aspirations and pursuits may well accord with yours. Each of us has our own karmic conditions, yet the single nostril within is fundamentally interconnected.
A congratulatory address for the Venerable Wuming, Elder of the Sangha Assembly of Shouyi, upon his sixtieth year:
The lineage of the Dao-pulse of Ehu extends afar; Six rings of the monk’s staff hang high above Aoyang. The leaders of all mountains recognize his compassionate virtue;

The people of this district take him as their bridge and raft, wafting the fragrance of the precepts. The mountain moon in the clear autumn is perfectly bright; The mountain pines in the height of summer are lush and verdant.
Vast and azure; the scenery of the four seasons is ever like a painting—all this is the Great Radiance of my Master’s long life.
In summer, I saw off the Venerable Miaozhan as he returned to his former retreat.

Departing from me amidst the humid heat, he said: "My home mountains may indeed be returned to; though my years are advanced, the world naturally grows cold toward me. My virtue is profound, yet my wisdom is all the more subtle."
The Mirror of the School hangs suspended in the void, pure; the lamp of the mind shines through the night. When shall we gather our heads once more to discuss the pivot of the arrow’s point?
To show purity and whiteness is to delight the multitude, yet people nourish their ailments while neglecting the Way.
Their vital energies are ever wanton and wild; when a single illness suddenly descends upon them, the pressure is such that it can hardly be borne.
The Way is the self-knowing of sickness; worldly thoughts have long since faded away. One looks only at the one who is not sick; as for the sickness, it returns to no particular place.
Both the sick and the one who is not sick are beyond measure; only then does one know that this mass of flesh is majestic and grand.
The Master Lànshēng, Làn Zàn, was indolent in wiping away his tears when meeting people; Làn Róng likewise did not rise when seeing others. These two elders were truly "lazy men" for all eternity;
who can compare with their lofty style? The Master’s religious name is Lànshēng; I do not know on what basis it was established.
This name truly captures the intent within indolence: lashing a clay ox to plow through fire.
In response to the verse by the lay practitioner Chen Jingji:
Within the distance of a few paces between Shigou and Rongcheng, who is it that comes to knock at the patriarch’s gate? Before birth, there was a poverty and...
Furthermore, to seek a mountain retreat while leaning toward the red dust of the world—this slightest stirring of a thought is the source of calamity.
Within this, the realm of reality is vast and expansive; once the eyes of the dream are opened wide, what could possibly exist?
The scorching heat of the burning house leaves one with a cold that penetrates to the very marrow of the bones.
Answered by Dharma Master Fu Li of Tang:

True Suchness does not maintain its own nature; it follows delusion and gives rise to false thoughts. The false and the true arise together; when one awakens to the truth, the false immediately ceases.
The place of cessation seems to have an end; in delusion, it is called beginningless. Though there is a distinction between delusion and awakening, the principle of suchness remains unmoving.
This is the art of returning to the source; by comprehending it, one transcends birth and death.
Presented to my Zen friend Chengxue upon his ordination:
The prajñā-sword is fundamentally sharp and keen; Its cold radiance constantly surges forth on its own. It tears asunder the net of the triple world, Releasing the monks of the Five Lakes.
Valleys and peaks are hidden beneath the brush; love and hate are exhausted within the breast. Amidst the long night of the lost path, you should strive to kindle the lamp of the mind.
Seeing you off as Master Sisheng returns to his old retreat:
Spring has passed and summer comes again as I return to the mountains. Gazing at clouds and sitting upon rocks, we have always been close. Before the crag, one must shout to sever the flow.
Water. On the ridge, I sweep away the dust until it is thoroughly moistened. Having already become mindless of going or staying, I know not where to seek greed and anger.
Out of pity for my old hidden cauldron, what harm is there in frequenting this place back and forth with my single staff?
Upon the arrival of the attendant Jìngzhǔ returning from Zǐyún to repair the Gānlù Precept Platform, this letter was sent to the venerable elders within the monastery:

Deep within Zǐyún, there are many sublime wonders; The precept platform has emerged from the earth, its ritual laws authentic. Its tiered levels, ascending and descending, all possess [their proper order].
Transcending, spirits and deities protect him; this too is not out of anger. Relying on the power of aspiration, he shall rebuild the new beams and rafters.
Heed not the talk of others to avoid the dust of worldly guests. As we part, my earnest exhortations leave nothing unsaid; wait but a moment to see the nectar once again renewed.
Inscription for the "Eight Immortals Assembling to Celebrate" Painting, Presented on the Occasion of Lady Miao Shi’s Seventieth Birthday:

When the peaches of the Queen Mother of the West are at their peak ripeness, The assembly of immortals gathers to celebrate this auspicious occasion. Though jade flowers and auspicious grasses are all brought forth, How can they compare to that single branch from the Lotus Pond?
Lady Shi has reached a noble age of seventy; Through lifelong fasting and the embroidery of Buddha images, her heart is pure.
Ever constant and one, the faculty of faith is planted within this pond. How could its lifespan ever have an end? At the clear dawn, celestial flowers drift down from afar;
fragrant breezes swirl about in rhythmic succession. Before the Elder Amitābha has yet opened his mouth, the flow of the Dharma resounds like thunder.
Upon hearing the Dharma, one immediately attains the stage of non-retrogression; with radiant marks and signs, one transcends the ordinary. Sea-house.
In the brief span of a moment, the tally was full. When compared to this man, he alone possesses a single countenance of serene composure.
To the Layman Zheng Yishui:

I envy you, who dwell in deep seclusion where no name is known; in your bamboo paths and thatched cottage, you find joy in yourself. Drinking water and resting your arm on a curved staff—who would recognize you?
Attained. The family tradition of the Confucian school possesses a true transmission.
To the Zen practitioner Yixing:
Samādhi is the ocean of sands; the lineage is singular. Mañjuśrī’s wisdom-mother teaches practice and cultivation; bind the conditions to the Dharma-realm and transcend birth.
In this very state, simply recollect Amitābha and you shall see your Original Teacher; within the world of the five turbidities, you will be pure to the very bottom.

Amidst the four modes of deportment, you sit in non-action (*wuwei*); from this, hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and patriarchs emerge. How could you fail to live up to this face given by your mother?
In the same rhyme, I respond to Director Yang Kanghou:

Since the time after [the Buddha] of the Golden Grain at Vaiśālī, Your illustrious name has long been admired and respected; Your calligraphy and ink-studies pervade the world, And I have had the opportunity to read them everywhere.

Winding my way, I entered Renbang, intending to pursue [the Way] constantly. Opening my eyes, I saw that the Path truly exists; I know my past affinities have long since ripened. He showed me an excellent composition;
our discussion was as effortless as splitting bamboo. Singing it aloud in the breeze, my joy was like that of one who has just bathed.
One day you shall surely sip from the Dragon Spring; I await you to boil the tripod-legged cauldron.
In summer, I sent back an elder of virtue, the old monk Ziyun, seventy years of age.
His staff is as lively as a dragon; he traveled far to the summit of Mount Ze. He did so precisely during the height of the sweltering heat.

With open hearts we discussed the ancestral Way; leaning our knees together, we spoke of our family traditions. Now you depart from me with a sudden turn; how many layers of green clouds and mountains lie before you?

As you leave my dwelling, I think of Master Ziyun, who is now elderly at home and remembers us from afar. He has frequently sent letters to Shimen. I wished to keep you here, yet could not detain you.
It is so. This state of mind is difficult to discuss with worldly people.

In the region of Quannan, the land of mulberry and lotus is uniquely possessed; recently, the mulberry and lotus have sprouted again. Not sparing body or mind, he diligently plants and cultivates them;
as spring arrives, the sacred blossoms grow everywhere.
On the fiftieth birthday of Lady Zhu, the mother of Mr. Huang:
The lifespan of Amitābha is originally immeasurable; The mother’s mindfulness of Amitābha is likewise so. The Pure Land is never separate from the five turbidities;
One must know that every step treads upon the green lotus.
Eulogy for Huang Jinggu of Wenling It has been nearly a year since I parted from the Master;
my heart has often drifted toward the edge of the Purple Clouds.
Suddenly hearing that he has taken his final leave of the world, I shed tears like autumn winds dripping onto round dewdrops.
What has been the outcome of my lifelong study of the Buddha? Birth and death cannot be defiled by external causes.
Throughout the comings and goings of over seventy years, it is like a single cloud unfolding and rolling up amidst the pines and vines.
Master Huayan has spent his entire life eating only Fucheng salt; with the harmony of many mouths, his physical strength and complexion remain firm. How shall I repay the kindness of the donors?
With three full meals, I have thoroughly investigated the five flavors of Chan.
The assembly of cloud-dwelling monks atop Shigufeng Peak share a meal of boiled green shepherd’s purse and white rice;
if donors would but provide salt and sauce, the flavor of these vegetable roots will be found all the more enduring.
Master Tang Bo’an sent me a poem; I respond in the same rhyme:
The illusory world is vast and boundless, yet when one fixes the gaze, the shore is found and one returns home. Within the dark chamber lies the treasure of true nature;

its application brings forth the spring blossoms upon the trees before one’s face. The path of the sages and the ways of the common folk are entirely fused and fundamentally non-dual; the holy and the ordinary are one body from the beginning.
It is not far; at the crown of his head he perfectly possesses the eye of Maheśvara. On dry land, what prevents him from sailing his raft?
To the parents of Layman Lindan Zhang on their double anniversary:
plants and trees welcome the fragrant breeze, and auspicious colors flourish. Their immortal forms and Buddha-bones are equally firm; their harmony of voice is like that of the *Guanju* bird.

The birds’ exquisite forms respond like lotuses sharing a single stem; beneath the steps, orchids and fragrant herbs nurture his aspirations. Within the hall, as days and months pass, he has long forgotten the passage of years.
Counting the cycles of the *huaxia* from the beginning, they have spread out a grand banquet for the Three Mountains to celebrate his longevity.
Inscription on the Ten Scenic Views of Longshan by Chan Master Gusue The Dharma King’s Peak rises far above a thousand peaks;
Majestic and towering, its form stands alone supreme. Contemplate deeply the Dharma of the Dharma King: Flowers fall like rain, filling the Jetavana Grove.
Where the many peaks of the Flame-Peak Mountain are about to break off, a solitary peak rises once more. The light of the mind remains ever-bright; there is no need to stir the cold ashes.
— *Bàngyuetai* (Platform for Beating the Moon)
The staff falls upon the moon in the void; let him wander along the walls as he may. It compels the man at the foot of the steps to emerge here from the birthless.
The cloud-protecting screen is originally a mindless thing; it drifts as if wishing to leave the mountain, yet one screen stands across to block it, refusing to open its gate.

In the Qianlong Pond, Hengyang is currently suffering from a severe drought; the great earth looks toward the clouds for relief. It is difficult for one who dwells in a secluded valley to remain settled forever; in the end, he shall surely soar across the azure heavens.
Jinji Cave.
The place where the ancients attained the Way has also earned a fine name for its caverns. Within the great dream of this floating life, one occasionally hears a single cry.

Amidst the clouds of Teng-kong Ridge, a bird-path stretches across; with its hundred turns, it opens spontaneously from heaven. For those who possess no selfishness beneath their feet, they may soar through the void, coming and going as they please.
The Listening Sutra Stone opens its great mouth in the void; day and night it spontaneously recites the sutra. Only the stone atop the mountain, spirit-like, is truly skilled at listening.
(Yaozu Rock)

The rocky crags were originally strange and beautiful, long hidden behind trailing vines and creepers. Now that they have been opened once more, the Way of the Patriarchs shines with renewed brilliance.
Within every nook of the Great Way lies the Great Way itself; it leads straight through to Chang’an. Let not those who would hide and evade remain forever attached to these green peaks.
Sent to my fellow practitioner Pan Shiyun, who has been appointed to Lingzhang:
For several years now, not a single letter has reached me. I imagine you have taken up the "ox-knife" merely to test your skill;
In handling the sinews and joints, you have well concealed your edge.

In the same rhyme as Layman Yú Chángyú: The rushing waters flow on, vying with one another to depart; The green mountains remain unchanged, year after year. A single meeting through the affinity of the Dharma is truly rare;
Yet our reunion at this ancient temple is once again radiant. The springtime of Máo Yǐn’s brush is ever in full bloom; The waves of his writing pour forth like jade.
Gurgling and flowing, the Lotus Society of Mount Kuanglu must surely not be silent; I further rejoice that Zong and Lei have entered the lecture hall.
To solicit funds for the restoration of the *Tripitaka* bestowed by Imperial Decree upon Zhiti Mountain:

the subtle words of the Tripiṭaka are the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom. Descended from the Nine Heavens, they are held in the utmost reverence; today, their restoration shall proceed in due order.
Adorned with the merit and wisdom of perpetual rebirth, this is entrusted to the layman Tang Bobian.
Before the parents were yet born, it was clearly just this very thing; yet as soon as a thought arose with the desire to take it up, one had already missed it face-to-face.
A mote of dust is not small at all; empty space is not large either. Birth and death are bubbles in water; Buddhas and Patriarchs are spit upon in the Pure Land.
Originally there was not a single thing; to deliberate otherwise is merely to increase one's confusion. Only the old master Xiangyan, striking the bamboo, had it suddenly burst asunder.
What, ultimately, is it? *Tut!* In response to the Chan Master Qingxi Hanzhao’s poem sent to me:
For ten years I have not heard of your place of seclusion; Your excellent news comforts me—how boundless is my joy! I have utterly abandoned the artifice of literary ornamentation.

In his practice, he exerts his full pen-power with the talent of one who binds a tiger; having attained the true flavor, his Way on the clouded mountains is lofty. Following conditions, whether in seclusion or in the world, his reflections are far-reaching.
In these times, the ocean of Dharma is especially defiled by corpses and filth; cherish the pure stream that is free from even a speck of dust.
Inscribed on the Water-Drawing Cliff:
A Steep Wall Carved Open by Heaven, Like the Gorges of Ba. The raging torrent roars long within these mountains. Who says that water is an insentient thing?
A single exhortation to turn back, and ten thousand sounds fall silent.
On a Summer Day, following the original rhyme, in response to the gift of verse by the Layman Xiayao-yuan upon visiting the mountains:
My humble learning is fragmented and I have lost my guiding principle; yet your refined and elegant style is uniquely dignified.

You have found your delight in tending the chrysanthemums in the garden, and now, braving the summer heat, you have come to visit me on this mountain. In this sagely age, who else could match the splendor of a phoenix? It is from this thatched cottage that the Way truly arises.
The Hidden Dragon. At the depths of the spiritual source, he personally wanders; there is no need for further cultivation of offerings to strange rocks.
Amidst the four dignified postures, he walks through the mountains; his steps are light. He contemplates the myriad phenomena, witnessing their own decay and flourishing.
Dwelling in the mountains, free from discursive thought, simply following conditions as one does in a guest house;
sitting in the mountains, the void is shattered, transcending Buddhas and patriarchs—there is only this.
Lying amidst the mountains, the heavens and earth are vast; man is not so. Few guests pass by.
Rejoicing in the rain (according to the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*, the Boundless Dragon King is the sovereign of the dragons of the trichiliocosm):
The Boundless Dragon rises to spread clouds of compassion; the rain falls upon Jambudvīpa, dividing in four directions. The fields and plains of the great earth are all already [flooded].
Sufficient! The signs of Great Peace are manifest, heard throughout the heavens.
We thank Master Zhuan’an for requesting him to reside at Shouchang, the home of the Dharma within the Yellow Dragon Peaks.
The withered tree has once again blossomed with the *utpala* flower; we pray that his descendants may be capable and effective.
Verse: One must still go and ask Old Xiqia:
"The colt tramples the people of the world to death; Huanglong revives the guests of the world. The vast waters flow freely, encompassing all;
Behold your commands of killing and reviving, renewed. (At that time, Master Gong was responding to the invitation to Shanglan.)
When the Venerable Shuidan’s pivot of the occasion did not manifest, how could the mechanism of this very person ever be obstructed?
Behold: light is constantly emitted through the six gates; the earth is stabilized and the heavens revolved as the axle frequently turns.
Transcending the present and surpassing antiquity, he gallops forth in full stride; the sun and moon vie to race alongside him at the borders of Han, while cold and heat compete in the human world.
Warm and cool; the Great Function is fundamentally without concealment or manifestation. It is only because of dream-visions that it is obscured.
On the birthday of the practitioner Zheng, I entered the mountains and composed this poem in response:
These dream-visions originally number neither a few nor a thousand. This year’s year is last year’s year. The body is like a mass of foam, manifesting as emptiness.

The Substantive: It is called "resembling a mad wind" as it stirs delusive conditions; ten thousand trees take on the hue of autumn and grow thin of themselves, yet the solitary peak, touched by the rain, appears all the more fresh.
If you wish to know true longevity, which is neither born nor extinguished, try looking at that which vaguely precedes even the Lord of Images.
Mian Hanhui, the *vina* (steward), sat long in meditation within the Kumu Hall; yet he was needlessly entangled by his own perceptions and views.

He spent his efforts vainly gathering up doorways and thresholds, wandering in vain through wild taverns and solitary villages. To have anything attained is ultimately an error; it is only when there is no place to rest that one truly begins.
Delusive conditions: the true message from beyond the limit of Vimalacitra can only be transmitted by those of transcendent character.
Exhorting the Chan practitioner Daoguo:

when setting out on a pilgrimage, the very first step is most critical. Having traveled a thousand li, the task is not difficult; one who can swallow the ocean of teachings and the river of Chan is truly capable.
[The land] was completely exhausted; only then did it become capable of producing waves upon level ground.
When a neighbor buried a thief in the lower courtyard of the temple, the dragon-lord (the guardian spirit) manifested its presence.
Consequently, the thief was moved away by official authority, and a poem was inscribed upon a stone to warn against those who might covet the site in the future.
For successive reigns, prayers have been offered for the Emperor’s ten-thousand-year longevity; how could these stinking bones be permitted to defile this place?
Since the hidden merit has been harmed and the heart-ground ruined, both the deceased and the living shall suffer retribution—this matter is no trivial one.
To bury a grave behind a temple or before a shrine brings ruin upon one's descendants with staggering frequency. How many such cases have I witnessed before my very eyes?
I leave this inscription today specifically to warn you.
The Chan practitioner Wuya requested a verse;

I show him this Great Way, which is fundamentally boundless. Encountering people, how could there be any exhaustion? Having sought south for fifty-three years, he treads upon emptiness, creating distance and proximity.
Returning, I saw Mañjuśrī; only then did I realize there was not the slightest thing lacking. Within a single pore of Samantabhadra, many beings have already attained Buddhahood.

For the sixtieth birthday of the layman Tao Zhengshu—a venerable elder—this person [the author] came at times to the midst of White Clouds to knock upon my gate of cultivation. For him, I spoke of the principles of the Western Land.

Upon hearing this, the Duke immediately accepted it with faith. With a smile that revealed his whiskers, he rejoiced; with fierce resolve, he renounced meat and pungent flavors, and through pure fasting, he was able to master himself.

Now, on this day, the archer’s bow is suspended; the first month of spring has come to its full beauty. In the high hall, a magnificent banquet is spread, and sons and grandsons bow in endless succession.
I am originally a man outside of things; there is no thing capable of being held as a likeness. Master Shou is Amitāyus; the lotus flower emerges from the mud.
A man of Ryūkyū sought the two-character verse on "Illusory Buddha":
"All Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally illusory; the great earth, mountains, and rivers are also illusory. If a person can recognize the pivot of illusion..."
At this juncture, one finally realizes that illusion is fundamentally not illusion.
Who is the Buddha? Who am I? Within this, turn it over and examine it closely. One day, seeing his face directly for oneself, one realizes that Confucius was originally Zhongni.

Manifesting the wandering of Jin-sheng, the eminent talent; in days of yore, Confucius gathered the great achievement. Resounding is the wooden clapper, vibrating with golden sound; the three fundamental relationships are established, making known the human race.

The Six Arts were edited and refined to demonstrate the course of law; the Way penetrates the eras of Tang and Yu, the mind being non-dual. His teaching fills the heavens and earth, its principle unerring.
He was especially refined in this; the true pivot of the Way has not yet perished. With a single thought free from self-interest, he continues the sagely brilliance.
To the Layman Qiu Xiyi:
Within the vast expanse of the universe, both noble and base have their destiny. Is this not granted by Heaven? It is determined by oneself.
Therefore, the wise person should be cautious regarding both transgression and merit; they do not merely scheme for the present, but deeply penetrate the path of the three periods of time.
Master Qiu was originally of a transcendent nature; his form and spirit were naturally serene and still. When he saw a guest, he would not even open his eyes, yet his mind was as clear as a mirror.
He suspended judgment on death and life; he minutely examined decline and prosperity. Not even a hair’s breadth was ever mistaken. Princes and dukes all listened with pleasure.

Those in the world who do not accept their fate wander aimlessly upon perilous paths. Only when they lose their footing and return home do they find that the four mountains have already closed in darkness.
When you visited me in the mountains, a single thought of right faith arose within you. You vowed to receive the precepts of refuge; you shall surely realize the fruit of Bodhi.
From now on, when encountering others, there is no need for further deliberation or judgment. If anyone asks about the art of shaping one's destiny, simply advance with this principle.
Master Wenjing (Wenyue Lengyan) of Shousanglian: Though dwelling in the secular world, he remains untainted by its dust;
donning the black robes, his cultivation of the Way grows ever more intimate. The white lotus is a worthy place to set one’s feet; this golden ground is where the spirit finds its rest.
How could my gaze perceive the river as different? Yet with each passing year, the world appears renewed. Having just finished reciting the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I have unconsciously changed watches.
**Warning the World (Two Poems)** The three realms are clearly but a single theater;
Each actor upon the stage displays his own strength. As the night draws to a close, the drums and gongs suddenly cease.
Alas! It merely causes bystanders to discuss merits and faults.
Born in Jambudvīpa, one does not study the Way; all day long, one busily seeks it outwardly. Even if one were to seek it until the end, what would it avail?
It is a pity to discard gold while carrying straw on one's back.
To Layman Jie’an of Helin (Two Poems) Seeking out an old monk in quietude, I sit cross-legged; As we debate, the wind arises—whom else can hear it?
Only the pines and stones upon the mountain peak Nod their heads from time to time, understanding my thoughts.

All beings who receive physical form possess a life span; when ten thousand coins are laid upon the table, who can truly fathom it? Let birds and fish be released to return to the heavens and the sea;
may the benevolent ones remain serene and each compose a poem.
The King has a virtuous official friend, the first of sixty, who has recently begun reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and has written this as a benediction:
"From early youth, he was endowed with adamantine bones; he knows that the indestructible body takes the dust of the earth as its measure of longevity, bearing the original truth of karma."
The three carts outside the gate are old; the single treasure within the robe is new. Its pure radiance shines eternally; its auspicious vapor naturally pervades all.

[Two Poems on the Fishing Line and Bamboo] Who would take up a fishing rod amidst the green mountains? To seek fish by climbing a tree is utterly absurd. Why not simply cast a net that covers the heavens?
The Net: Difficult to escape from those traveling by water, land, or air.
With no bait on the hook, he draws in tortoises and crocodiles. He also drags the line across the ground. One who has not tasted the flavor comes to the hook.
The Old Man of Huating laughs heartily.
Hearing that my nephew, the Chan Master, had entered the mountains, I have composed this verse in his style to welcome him as he comes along the path from Shitou.
Traversing a thousand miles, you have arrived at the mountain’s edge; Ten years of parting, vast as the sea, are now ended.
In our single meeting, our hearts converse like thunder; I know you can uphold the Dharma with profound secrecy, Yet I am ashamed of my own ineptitude in aiding the times.
The Forge and Hammer. In the depths of fine mountains, many numinous trees grow; their branches reach toward heaven, relying on deep nourishment.
Presented to the Venerable Xiqian as he returns to the Western Regions:

having traversed snow-capped peaks and shifting sands, you have journeyed ten thousand miles from afar to reach the Middle Kingdom. Yet you do not seek the Great Dharma for the sake of saving sentient beings.
Death! To linger in gazing at the waters and mountains is a great mistake.
The Eastern Land and the Western Heaven share but one continent; you have traveled far on your own, with your water jar and staff.
Now that you wish to return to the West once more, do not lose sight of the path by which you came.
Verses on Indicating the Brahma-Bead Venerable Vinaya Master (Two Poems) The Great Way is fundamentally without front or back;
To seek the Great Way is itself to lose the path. Not seeking, yet one falls into the realm of ignorance;
A sudden awakening restores one to the status of a great man.
The customs of the age are thin and evil, unfit for intimacy; in setting one’s resolve, one must emulate the ancients.
Exert yourself with meticulous care lest you err, and do not allow a speck of gold-dust to enter your eye.
Presented to Layman Zeng Changzhong (Two Poems) For three years you have not eaten the flesh of sentient beings;
In every thought, maintain sincerity to repay your mother’s kindness. Remember well your many parents throughout countless lifetimes;
With a single mind, deliver them all together into the Gate of Compassion.
The three realms are blazing with heat; this is truly a house on fire. Who will awaken with such vigor as to seek cool relief? Amitābha constantly extends his hand everywhere;
if one knows how to take refuge in a single thought, that is the Land of Bliss.
Presented to Layman Peng Erren (Two Poems) Truly coming from the cliffs of Putuo, Brothers, you have entered the womb by virtue of your vows.
Indeed, you have not lost your way back; Twin lotuses bloom amidst the flames.

The myriad differences in daily life are all delusions; not knowing where else to seek the truth, if one attains clear awakening to the essential point within this very state, the flowering of blossoms on an iron tree is a spring unlike any other.
Ascending Lizi Peak (with Preface):

It has been ten years since I last ascended the summit. In the autumn of the Dingwei year of the Kangxi era, Master Wuke of Qingyuan happened to bring Fang Tianbo and several other gentlemen into the mountains;
we subsequently made an appointment to travel together. On that day, the persistent rain had just cleared.

The weather was clear and bright; ten thousand peaks stood arrayed, vying with one another in their wondrous and exquisite beauty. Gazing eastward toward the great sea, it stretched out boundlessly, a vast expanse of white.
We sat upon the rocks brewing tea, our laughter and conversation ringing coolly in the air. Shortly thereafter, a gentle breeze arose from the northeast;
unable to withstand the cold, Master Ke departed first and returned home. I, for my part, again invited my companions to exhaust the pleasures of Fengchi.
By the time we returned, the sun was already kissing the mountain peaks. Master Ke had already completed his poem and shown it to me;
I have composed two verses in response to record the inspiration of that moment.
Lofty and towering, the peaks rise abruptly; a winding path leads far into the distance. Ten thousand crags compete to stand below, while two rivers vie to flow toward the east.
The sun and moon are seen racing past; heaven and earth are like whirling tumbleweeds. Why have you not come for ten years? My body remains within these mountains.
Dwelling in the mountains, I did not see the mountains; long have I neglected this climbing. When the Master arrived, he was able to summon me; when the heavens opened, my face broke into a smile.

Grass fragrance and tea are boiled together; ancient characters on stone are not inert. Surveying at one glance the seas and mountains to their end, I ride the wind and return with sleeves brushed clean.

*Inscription on the Waterfall at Qingyuan (with Preface)* The second year after Chan Master Wuko took up residence at Qingyuan, he discovered a three-tiered waterfall at the source of the eastern stream.
Fubao has revealed a secret of a thousand years; it is truly marvelous and extraordinary. I offer this verse as a gift:
A source of ten-thousand bushels of spring water suddenly bursts open, Three lengths of white silk cascade down from the Cloud Terrace.
For many years it was hidden in a place where no one dwelt, Yet now it has been led forth by one who is himself without a person.
To Layman Zhang Zaihui on Pure Land Practice:
The Western Pure Land lies ten trillion lands away, yet it resides solely within a single thought-moment of the person themselves.
When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is naturally pure; where could Amitābha not be encountered?
As soon as one reaches the Western Land, the flowers bloom; having personally received the prediction of enlightenment, one sheds the ordinary mortal frame.
Turning the body around, one enters universally into worlds as numerous as dust motes, extensively welcoming all sentient beings—come and go!
Praise for Śākyamuni Tathāgata Holding His Alms Bowl:
Originally an old bhikṣu from the Western Heaven, He donned his robes and carried his bowl with refined elegance, Wandering through long streets and narrow alleys.
Depart! For the sake of all sentient beings, you have forcibly emerged from the head.

The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion praises the Dharma-realm as the True Body; the myriad phenomena serve as its hands and eyes. Even empty space may yet be measured, but these hands and eyes can never be numbered.
For the sake of inferior sentient beings, I have briefly shown only one thousand;

yet even with a single hand and eye, one would still be unable to exhaustively rescue all sentient beings of the great earth, let alone with a thousand hands and eyes. The Great Being’s unconditioned compassion is equal toward all sentient beings.

The minds of sentient beings are inexhaustible, and thus compassion is likewise inexhaustible. To recite the name for even a single thought-moment, the entire body [of the Buddha] manifests before one.
With this manifest mind, I praise the manifest Great Being; it is like space merging with space—a single characteristic without duality.

Eulogy for the Purple Mushroom Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (With Preface) A guest presented me with a single purple mushroom, which clearly depicted the Great Being Avalokiteśvara seated in a reclined posture upon Mount Potalaka.
He held a pure flask in his hand, and all his auspicious marks were fully manifest. Thereupon, I was moved by the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded great compassion and followed [this inspiration].
All things assume their forms; this is inconceivable. With reverent purification, I prostrate and offer praise.
As I observe this fungus, it has grown from the great earth; yet from where does the form and countenance of the Great Being come? By this, one knows the Bodhisattva.
With unimpeded great compassion, he manifests his presence everywhere, like the moon reflected in a pond. Upon each gaze and each prostration, one should make this vow:
"May I become a transformation Buddha who adapts to the various types of beings, remaining free from attachment and craving."
Praise of Water-Moon Avalokiteśvara:
The moon in the water is the moon at the edge of the sky; The illusory transformation body is the Dharma-nature body.
Moment by moment, turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature— Avalokiteśvara has never been anyone else.

I praise Cundī Bodhisattva, who observes that the Bodhisattva is fundamentally without body, yet manifests her form everywhere to bestow blessings upon all beings. Her three eyes shine perfectly, neither vertical nor horizontal;
her eighteen arms hold various implements. Whether through compassion or majesty, she extensively gathers and sustains all, [the power] of seventy million Buddhas.
The one who is the Teacher, for whom the world calls "Mother of Buddhas," who encompasses and nurtures all without exception;

the one who proclaims the divine mantras as the sovereign of the five families, whose protection and salvation of sentient beings are most vast; who wards off calamities and grants blessings such that the response is immediate, like an image appearing in a mirror without interval;
whose unconditioned, wondrous virtue is inconceivable—I compose these words of praise to fathom the ocean with a conch-shell spoon. May it only be that...

Beholding these signs, they give rise to faith and are gathered into the vast and profound ocean of vows. They fulfill bodhi through non-attainment, just as Bodhisattvas bring blessings to all beings.
The two devas, Sankha and Gopa, praised the sons of heaven of the form realm and the desire realm.
With Sankha and Gopa as their leaders, they followed the Buddha into Mount Potalaka, where they joined the Dharma assembly together with the multitude of bodhisattvas.
There, they personally beheld the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara, who secretly manifested great supernatural powers.
Radiant light shone forth and boundless buddha-fields all trembled; one knew that he was about to proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Indeed, having heard this vast *dhāraṇī*, the entire assembly attained realization. This person and this Dharma are truly inconceivable;

therefore, they again questioned him regarding his physical appearance. The Great Being revealed himself with a heart of great compassion—equanimous, unconditioned, and free from attachment—and likewise [without]...
Amidst disorder and affliction, they remain humble and respectful toward all. Their unsurpassed bodhicitta is supreme;
it guides the deluded throughout the entire dharmadhātu, extensively performing various deeds of benefit. Yet the very nature of their mind is inherently empty and quiescent.
Upon hearing this, Mahābrahmā was immediately relieved; to this day, he has upheld it without forgetting. Its subtle, secret, and profound realization is unfathomable.
He then again manifested the form of a celestial being and entered together with the hosts of devas into the dharma assemblies of all Tathāgatas.
He protects and upholds those practitioners who recite mantras, causing all their aspirations to be fulfilled. His boundless merit—

Sublime and inconceivable, he is no different from Avalokiteśvara. I have composed these words of praise to describe but a small fraction of his qualities, like a single opening in the sky or a single drop in the ocean.
—Eulogy by the Elder Master Míyún Tiāntóng.
Atop the peak of Tongguan Mountain, it manifests with brilliant clarity; white staffs crisscross, facing every direction without front or back.

When I entered the room in the past, I believed this immediately without doubt; yet now, as I reflect upon it, how could it be anything less than a blade of mugwort? The Great White [Peak] rises a thousand fathoms, piercing straight through the azure heavens.
Behold it, look up to it! Lofty is the Land of the East (Zhendan).
The Elder of Gushan praises the single drop of blood from Shouchang as ten-thousand-fathom waves at Caoxi. Standing alone within the Jambudvīpa realm, its resonance is naturally harmonious.
A single hair preserves the thousand sages; a solitary mind is entrusted to the *bìluó* vines. Who knows this intent? The old Bodhidharma from the West.
Master Tianhua Shiyu praises fishing and releasing living beings:
"The power to kill and bring to life is already complete; he hands over a single broken fly-whisk directly before one's face. For more than thirty years."
Celestial flowers fall like rain; from the roots and stumps of ordinary trees, extraordinary sprouts emerge. Their lush, spreading branches resemble those of the Jambū tree.
In praise of Master Juede of Lingyin (with an introduction):
The name "Lingyin" has long resounded in my ears. Today, upon this painting, I have suddenly encountered it face-to-face.
Beholding his countenance and demeanor, his celestial form was solemn as he presided over the assembly of devas and humans.

He was one who skillfully employed the "blind donkey" technique to extinguish the orthodox lineage of Linji; that the gate of Dayu Sanfeng should be established throughout the world for future generations—who else but this Master could have accomplished this?
The abundance of his disciples and the flourishing of his karmic conditions were merely incidental matters for the Master. From the East [the land of] Lu...
At the request of Chan Master Ming, I respectfully inscribe these few words of praise:
The Dharma of the mind is formless; its virtues are immeasurable. When there is need, it is employed; what hindrance or obstruction could there be? Thus was the Linji school established.
The treasury of the True Dharma is extinguished. Who is this? It is the Venerable Master Lingyin.
My elder brother Xueqiao praised his early attendance at the Chan assembly;
he has long served in various positions within the monastic community. By nature he is fundamentally open and unobstructed; he neither clings to things nor insists on his own way.
Thus, those who hear of him rejoice and those who see him are gladdened; those who draw near receive benefit.

Having finally received the *vinaya* of his former teacher, he stood as a solemn model for the entire assembly. Yet, before his profound treasury of wisdom could be fully unfolded, he suddenly hastened toward *nirvāṇa*.
What cause for regret is there in this for our Master? It is only a matter of deep sorrow for the Dharma-gate.
Three years had passed since the passing of the Venerable Master Luan of Dongluan.
When his coffin was opened for the cremation, his physical body remained intact and undecayed.
Among those who choose Buddhahood in the midst of Shigushan, wife and children were cast away like fine dust. No one recognized his karmic deeds during life;
yet after death, he was able to leave behind an indestructible body.
A Chan Abbot’s Song of Praise for Walking Meditation:
Before the towering peaks of Xiling, he sits cross-legged. His practice inherits Yangqi; his robes are those of Bodhidharma. In silence, he spontaneously speaks of non-arising.
Fortunately, there are stubborn rocks with whom to sing in harmony. A single smile reveals the wondrous mechanism before all else. Mountains and rivers are vast.
The earth encompasses him entirely.
This eulogy for my elder brother, composed by Daoxiong, entrusts his essence to the waters of Jian.
He was nurtured amidst the refined beauty of Mount Zhi; he harmonized with all things through joy and kept his mind in tranquil stillness. He was courageous in his pursuit of pure karma.
Diligent in the field of merit, dwelling within the world of the five turbidities like a lotus emerging from the water— if one speaks of such a teacher,
they may truly be called a preeminent figure among the Sangha and a precious vessel beyond the mundane world.

The venerable elder Jinggong of Yixiang entered the chamber of Boshan at an early age and personally studied under the Caodong school of Chan. As his years advanced, his mind grew ever more robust; through the changes of the world, his resolve became even firmer.
The moon of precepts hangs in the sky, pure; the clouds of compassion shade all things, perfect. Returning to Shigou in the evening, her voice and radiance illuminate the great thousandfold world.

Master Huiyun praised this old nun: "From her youth she was endowed with merit and wisdom; she left home at the age of seven and immediately excelled her peers. Once her virtue in the precepts was perfected—"

The sharpness of his wisdom was keen; there was no matter he did not master and no principle to which he did not penetrate. He served as a guide for the multitude, with the purification of karma as his primary aspiration.

He extensively transformed those with whom he shared a karmic affinity, leading them all together to the ground of enlightenment. Having exceeded sixty years of age, he departed from the assembly and passed away. Both the ordained and the laity held his character in deep reverence.

Alas! Tears flow down my face; the remaining image stands solemn and majestic. May blessings be perpetually bestowed upon those like you. With incense by day and lamps by night, may you hope to be free from shame.

Layman Lin Wenruo praised the planting of roots of goodness in the diamond ground of the past; the fruit of merit is now perfected in the Jeta Grove. Do not say that robes and capes alone lead one to aspire for the immortals.
Traces. One should know that the mind is the Buddha-mind.
A verse of praise for the conduct and joy of my fellow practitioner Zheng Junheng:

"Tearing his robes, he traversed the peaks of ten thousand mountains; returning from gathering medicinal herbs, his countenance was radiant. He dwells eternally amidst the dust, yet the dust does not [defile him]."
[He was] defiled. This very body is that of an earth-walking immortal (*bhūcarī-ṛṣi*).
The Daoist friend Yuxu praised this old man: "His beard and hair are white;
he walks with a direct mind and acts with direct conduct. Every thought is a blessing and a condition for merit; he purchased fields to provide food for the monks."

He fired tiles to roof the hall and practiced repentance for three years, whereupon peace was visibly realized. Such deeds as these are difficult for others to perform, yet he accomplished them with ease and laughter through the power of his vows.
I know this gentleman to be a mass of merit and virtue who extensively welcomes those with whom he has a karmic affinity.
We share the same path toward enlightenment.

I have heard that the Elder praises the lotus as the heart and the vajra as the bones; dwelling amidst the dust without being stained, and facing adversity without being disgraced, its essence is free from self.
I. Blooming flowers on ancient trees; employing a hearing that has never heard before. Sounds are transmitted through the empty valley; who can know their celestial forms and Daoist countenances?
With a single casual stroke, they are all brought forth.
Huālín Xīnyī, a man of venerable virtue, praised me for having known Master Wù for over thirty years. As the years have passed, his resolve remains unchanged. Deep within Huālín...

I respectfully close my meditation chamber to unroll the sutras and recite the Buddha’s name. The fragrance of his virtue and deeds flows afar; though he stands on the verge of seventy years, his heart remains like that of an infant.

With a manner of easy laughter and gentle harmony, he receives all beings with the utmost universality. Dwelling in the midst of the mundane world, he remains unstained; the Pure Land is his aspiration, standing tall and solitary beyond the realm of things.
The White-Browed One Among the Sangha.
Li Jin’s *Praise for the Upāsikā Nǚ* (with Preface).
Good son Guǎn Shìmín, of noble lineage, [composed this] in honor of the compassionate Lady Nǚ, an upāsikā whose dharma name is Jīn.
Cease. For over twenty years, she has observed the fasts and recited the Buddha’s name.

Now that she has reached her seventies, on her birthday she has specifically entered the mountains to provide a meal for the monks and request the Dharma, thereby expressing her auspicious wishes for the Nanshan tradition. Furthermore, she has brought a portrait of the Master to request a eulogy.
I consider this: the two sons’ filial hearts toward their mother are themselves the mother’s own heart of mindfulness of the Buddha. The Buddha, in turn, remembers the mother...

The mind is precisely the mother’s heart that loves her two children; thus, when the child is filial toward the mother, the mother will surely attain longevity, and when the mother recites the Buddha’s name, she will certainly behold the Buddha.
This is because these two states arise from the ultimate nature (zhi-xing);
they cannot be tainted by human artifice. Observe his dignified countenance and celestial form as he sits cross-legged upon a round mat of *pó* grass.
A mani-jewel rests in her hand; a scripture lies upon her desk. A young maiden stands in attendance to her right, holding a staff.
Her demeanor is serene and detached; though her body remains in this Sahā world, her spirit has already journeyed to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. I respectfully compose a eulogy for her.
The shadow is straight because the form is upright; the trace flourishes because the root is exalted. Turning back to contemplate the source of form—how could one fall into mere appearances?

With a single stroke of brush and color, he has effortlessly portrayed it: the features are solemn and present, like the crimson sun at the third watch. For twenty years, he has personally maintained the six-syllable Buddha-name.
The superior-grade jewel lotus is what he aspires to.
At the heart of the pond, the Daoist You transmitted these humble words of mine; I myself took up the staff, stood by his side, and respectfully offered these few lines of praise.
Upon the stone of Panṭa, a subtle smile appeared. Only this attendant could silently accord with the occasion. The father was young and the son was old;
though the whole world did not believe it, we two knew it within ourselves. It was fixed by our innate nature. The seeds of Bodhi were deeply planted upon the field of enlightenment.
Life after life, may we together serve as a bridge for others.
Master Jing of Juelin praised people for pursuing learning;
I do not accept this view, yet I alone value the Master’s lack of formal learning. While people vied with one another to discourse on Chan, [the Master remained indifferent].
I do not join them; rather, I alone join Master [Shou] who does not delight in Chan. This is because he does not speak of false speech, nor does he study false learning.
Thus, those far away are moved with longing, while those nearby are filled with joy. He has truly caused the precepts and Dharma of Boshan and Gushan to overflow throughout the Middle Kingdom.
As for those in the world who have the skin of a tiger but the nature of a sheep—delighting at the sight of grass yet finding their bellies utterly empty within—[he is not like them].

As for those who possess [the Dharma], how could they be anything less than separated by as vast a gulf as heaven and earth? Alas! In this age of the Final Dharma, the wind of the teaching has grown faint and the surging waves decline day by day;
thus, regarding my Master, I cannot help but harbor a sense of profound veneration.
The Chan practitioner Guangfude praises him:
Having escaped from the forest of spears and swords, he has recovered his life from amidst the surging waves. Turning back, he enters directly into the House of the Dharma King;
with a single heart of sincerity, he cultivates the true practice. His resolve is like a diamond, never to change; he refuses to paint over the void with idle words.

The five colors [of the lotus] rely solely upon the single phrase "Amitābha. Having crossed the boundless sea of birth and death, the fellow practitioner Yang Junrong praises his childhood days when they gathered sands together in play within the same neighborhood;
yet in middle age, meeting again, it was as if separated by an entire lifetime. Though their robes differ—monk and layman alike—[their bond remains].

The Way is fundamentally of one essence; entering deeply into the Dharma-gate, the mind of faith is non-dual. It is here that the image is depicted—not merely to represent outward form, but to capture the inner intent.
I have composed these verses of praise, awaiting the record of the Dragon Flower Assembly.

Kongsheng, a fellow practitioner of dhyāna, entered the Gate of Emptiness in his youth and remained there until old age; his resolve was steadfast and unyielding, and the Way of Gautama filled his moral character.

With a vast and open breast, his resentment vanished upon seeing me; his realization of the nature of things was profound. Recently he ascended Mount Shigou to personally receive the sublime precepts;
his vows and practices have become ever more expansive, and he has become a master vessel within the Dharma-gate.
Huiri, a fellow practitioner of Chan, was born into a distinguished clan.

He donned the white robes at Nanshan and from childhood until old age, maintained a single-minded resolve without backsliding. His mind was as simple as it was sincere, and his endeavors were characterized by diligent industry.
He received others with kindness and harmony, radiating a warmth like spring. With a single invocation of Amitābha, he brought all six sense faculties under complete mastery.
In both Sukhāvatī and Sahā, all alike return to the point of the falling snow.
Cloud-Gathering (Yunju) opened the mountain;

a public eulogy for his shedding of the white robe at Baiyunyan. Cloud-Gathering was the founder of the mountain: ancient countenance and ancient mind, true practice and true speech. In the empty mountains, he established a Buddhist monastery.

Reaching high toward the vault of heaven, it was achieved solely through the power of aspiration and the accumulation of merit over time. Having reached the age of seventy, the fruit of the Lotus Land ripened;
he passed away peacefully while seated, amidst a fragrant breeze. His portrait remains here, solemn and as if alive. O you who come after:
Successive deeds are performed without indolence.
Pan Qixi’s literary conduct and joyous character are praised;
his expansive and open breast was obtained from Heaven. His ambition for the four quarters of the world was not in vain. He stands tall and solitary amidst Jambudvīpa.
His robes and cap fluttered as he moved, appearing like an immortal.
Panshanzi, the filial and incorruptible scholar, praised him, saying:

"In his youth, he was naturally gifted with a profound mind; his filial piety and fraternal affection were innate. Once he reached adulthood, he achieved renown without exerting great effort; he regarded wealth and status as but floating clouds."
Life and death are like illusions and bubbles; they drift away as one enters this world. That which is not illusory remains eternally.

When the Master [Confucius] praised Hui and wept for him with such intensity, it was because his father missed his son and his heart could not forget him. Both instances arise from the same source: the nature of Heaven; they are fundamentally not the result of emotional compulsion.
Only this remains: to comfort you, my son, and to comfort me, your father. Behold the rising sun; it faces the east every single morning.

The old monk Huai Guang praises the ninety-year-old monk who has already forgotten all contrivance: his mind is like that of an infant, ignorant of a hundred things; there is only Amitābha constantly bound within his heart.
Recollection: His spirit has long dwelt within the precious lotus pond.
For over a dozen autumns, Bao-shan has internally illuminated the monastery and assisted the abbot with diligent devotion for the assembly;
his sincere heart, piece by piece, is truly without peer. The vows he has practiced throughout his life are as profound as—
The ocean is not stirred by the winds and waves of Māra;
at Peach Blossom Hermitage, the elder brother Jiacan personally beheld the ancient Buddha Shouchang.
With skin like ice and bones like snow, he is utterly free from even a speck of dust; having fulfilled his practice for ninety days, he has returned home.
He departed. Everywhere throughout the world, peach blossoms bloomed in profusion.

This eulogy of the venerable elder Qinglin’s spiritual image has entered all quarters to encompass them, and emerged from all quarters to encompass them. For thirty or fifty years, he hid in the east and fled to the west.
The Buddha’s traces are difficult to find elsewhere. At eighty-six years of age, he still holds fast to this single phrase, "Amitābha.
He earnestly recites it himself and teaches others to recite it as well. His rebirth in the Pure Land is as certain as water flowing eastward.
If one asks whether he is Chan or Pure Land, his teeth remain firmly clenched, showing not a hint of wind. Who is this person? This old, frozen lump at Shilin Hermitage.
Praise for Mr. Shao Jiantin, Grand Councilor of the Central Region:

Having attained the highest honors early in his career, he has served in every capacity. As Commander-in-Chief and Governor of Sichuan, he displayed the courage to sacrifice his life in the face of peril.
To this day, his meritorious deeds endure for the people; Mount Emei and its moon remain as perfectly pure as ever.
Eulogy for the Portrait of Master Lin Jiān:
Two thousand measures of grain are easily obtained; a single almsbowl is difficult to seek. To clarify the intent of transcending the world, one must first possess this head.
Song Jing spoke in vain of regret; Zhaozhou once said there was none. In the place where one burns incense and observes in stillness, the floating world undergoes its own prosperity and decay.
The Layman Daochong has long shared a karmic affinity for the Dharma with me; he thus painted two small portraits of us seated together upon pines and rocks.
On the Mid-Autumn Festival of the year Bingwu, he visited me again in the mountains and brought forth the painting for my inspection.
Unable to help it, I laughed aloud and respectfully inscribed these few words.

I know not in what age we first met; in this life, once again we have gathered together. Though we share pine trees and rocks in wordless silence, it is evident that both of us originally possess something.
But tell me, what is it? Majestic halls and stupas tower amidst the clouds; manifest throughout kalpas, they remain forever imperishable.
In Praise of the Five Pine Painting: A Commemoration for the Eightieth Birthday of the Layman Lin Yin (with Preface).

I established the Lotus Society in a detached precinct of this temple. I have always rejoiced in the entry of the local elders and worthies into the association, so that we might together cultivate friendships beyond the secular world.
The venerable layman Lin Yin of Lupu is one such individual. This year falls on the year of Yisi.
In the month of Chrysanthemums, on the day of the full moon, it coincided with the venerable elder’s eightieth birthday.

His son, Dezhimao, attended upon his staff and sandals to join the society and requested a colophon for the "Five Pine Trees" painting as a blessing for the elder’s Southern Mountain years. I could not decline.

The elder’s family had produced five distinguished officials across generations. From his childhood, he practiced the studies for the civil service examinations, but his efforts repeatedly failed, like a frost-bitten horse repeatedly stumbling.

He then resolutely declared, "What is the use of this mere droning? Thereupon, he delved into the secret strategies of Sun Wu and read them, saying, "This is the means by which one may achieve fame and merit.
He subsequently established martial achievements and was promoted to the rank of *youfu*. Later, he retired from office to seek refuge in the woods, where he did nothing but open [the scrolls].

There were three paths. He would often gather with his guests and friends for assemblies in the region north of the Yellow River; he instructed his children and grandchildren in poetry and the classics, while his servants tended to the mulberry trees and hemp.
Beyond these matters, there was no need to concern himself with worldly affairs or report on them.

Whenever the carriage of an elder entered the village, everyone would stop their carriage at the gate to inquire after him. As for his sons, daughters, grandsons, and great-grandchildren, they all gathered affectionately around his knees—altogether numbering four [generations].
In this world, the jade trees stand towering and the orchids flourish in competition; his advancement is but now beginning and shows no sign of ceasing.

Now, at eighty years of age, his countenance remains youthful and refined, while his crane-like hair flows gracefully. His sons and grandsons gather around the hall, offering cups to present their congratulations on his longevity.
People behold him and think that the Old Man of the Southern Pole has descended from the void, as a tide of joy surges forth.
Yang. His joy is boundless. Master Lin Hanzhai has painted a picture of the Five Pines to offer his felicitations.
He takes as his model those which flourish all the more amidst frost and snow, and maintain their integrity with steadfastness. The longevity of the future is inherently immeasurable;
how could it be limited merely to the "one hundred and ten years" (qūqū) of traditional expression? I respectfully compose this eulogy for him: [The eulogy follows.]

Five pines stand side by side, like coiled dragons and soaring serpents. Their roots wind around white stones; their forms reach out to pierce the azure heavens. Purple scales glisten in the sun; verdant crests chant with the wind.
Firm and steadfast by nature, they share in the power of the Great Transformation. Grasping at clouds and seizing mists, they soar loftily within the realm.
I cannot fathom the limits of his years; I shall briefly cite them here to honor this elder.
This noble layman possesses a magnanimous demeanor and a spirit of exceptional brilliance.
He wears the robes of a Confucian scholar yet harbors the mind of a Buddha at his core. He rejoices in the joys of others and grieves in their sorrows, and is capable of true compassion.

Free from malice and devoid of worldly seeking, his rank grew ever higher as his virtue became ever more profound. Having long attained mastery in the gates of Chan and Pure Land, he remained at the age of eighty with the countenance of a youth.
His solemn presence was as if alive, illuminating the ages for a thousand autumns.
Eulogy for the Elder Layman Xie Xiange: The Eastern Mountain excels in its refined beauty;

from the Gui Lin, branches have flourished. His family has transmitted the tradition of farming and study; his longevity has reached the age of one hundred. His son has already surpassed him in wisdom.
Sun Yu was precocious from his youth; his person was at ease and his mind leisurely, his nature tranquil and his spirit serene. He was a guest of the Imperial Academy, a model for the degenerate age.
Alas! Regarding such a man as this, I have nothing further by which to praise him.

Extensively proclaiming his venerable virtues and extolling his noble lineage, this patch-robed monk’s conduct and concealment have ultimately led him to ascend the Hall of the Stone Drum; there he cultivates Chan and Pure Land in perfect union.
Vowing to the Lotus Land, her pearl-like brilliance adorns the river’s beauty; the fragrance of her virtue and deeds flows forth, far transcending worldly entanglements.
Like the moon rising over the high ridge, all gaze up at her with reverence; her pure radiance is ever within sight.
Self-praise: Clouds atop the towering peaks of Xili; snow at the mouth of the Lingyuan Cave. With a single stroke, they are just finished; the celestial mechanism is fully revealed.
Should someone further ask whether it resembles [the original], it would be like driving another stake into empty space. Now, I lift it up and show it to you all.
People—let those who are angry be angry, let those who are pleased be pleased.
From Jambudvīpa in the south to Uttarakuru in the north, his countenance remains solemn and unchanged; why labor further to describe it?

Once it is depicted in ink and color, one cannot avoid mistaking a tortoise for a turtle. Attendant Xuán, you must look with a sudden flash of insight; do not allow another layer to be added to your eyes.
[The attendant Xuan stands by his side.
This master painter has painted this image to delude the people of the world; you have gone so far as to offer it worship.
Stop making offerings! Look at it before the brush has even been lifted—what kind of appearance is it?
This fellow truly lacks understanding; he regards fame and status as if they were hair being shaved off, and treats the Way of Chan as if it were filthy mud.
He is blunt and unrefined, dull-witted and ignorant. When someone asks him about the meaning of the Westward Journey, he simply pulls out that very thing from those years.
Branches. Clearly, half of them are not worth a single coin, yet it is said: "This is that which has never been transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs from above.
*Ei!* Old Stone Drum the Dhūta suddenly produces three feet of silk. Thus one knows that the firm and dense body manifests within all dust.
Everywhere one encounters him; it is difficult not to see him. His features are so solemn and majestic; space has no front or back.
(At the request of Master Puyin.)
Mountains join as clouds arise; the moon follows the wind in its course. If you wish to know the ultimate point, it is at midday and the third watch.
Before this has occurred, there is no tenfold manifestation. Once this has occurred, one calls a horse a hare; taking error for truth.
I shall provide you with a brief commentary: The Buddha is made of clay; the cauldron is cast of iron. What more need be asked? Blue skies give rise to mist.

This fellow is ignorant and fails to recognize the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If he is willing to acknowledge it himself and has confidence in himself, let no one obstruct him. He reviles the teachings and destroys the lineage.
They disparage the present and belittle the past; they point to earth as gold and point to gold as earth. Utterly inverted and topsy-turvy—who could possibly be their peer?
Being such unrefined fellows, they deserve only to be banished to a world where no Buddha dwells, left to whatever slanders and praises others may utter.
Why was he brought forth from the Patriarchal Hall to be included among the one thousand seven hundred [great masters] (as requested by Ling Shi)?
Zhi Guang, a man of venerable virtue, hailed from a distinguished clan;
he donned the white robes at Putuo and deeply explored the river of Chan at Boshan and Tiantong. In his later years, he came to Shigou.
The splendor of the Sahā world is shrouded; the remaining radiance is eclipsed and obscured. Amidst the misty haze of pines and cypresses, is he alive or dead?
Upon the moonlit isles and wind-swept branches, his countenance remains solemn and vivid. Lofty and towering are the high mountains.
As General-in-Chief, he performed the duties of a Prince (with a formal narrative):
he received the Imperial mandate before the Crown Prince, leading ten thousand troops and striking awe throughout the realm.

He resided in Fuzhou for five years, visiting me twice in the mountains. He resolved my difficulties and dispelled my doubts, never failing to express his admiration by clapping his hands in approval as he poured forth the depths of his inner realization.
He would leave behind poems before departing. Suddenly, one day, he passed away without illness, causing shock and commotion throughout both the court and the commonalty.
I remarked that the public’s benefit from his virtue and grace lay with the military and the people, while his meritorious achievements remained for the sake of the state. Furthermore—
There exists that which undergoes birth and death without changing, and penetrates heaven and earth without being worn away. How could you, sir, truly die?
I respectfully compose this eulogy to entrust to your eldest son, Yu, who is surely one capable of perpetuating his family’s legacy. The eulogy says:

O, Sovereign and Duke! A dragon among men, tall and stately, solemn and reverent. Endowed with the nature of the virtuous and the good, possessing both complete talent and martial prowess, you are an auspicious omen for the state and a support to the King.
